352|    scores = REC.call("weights", _weights, (self, scores), {})
353|    if REC.census_on:

355|    y = self.experts(x, inds)

453|def prefill(model, ids, cache):
454|    """Run the prompts *ids* into *cache* and return the first new tokens.
455|
456|    The prompts run in chunks of at most PREFILL_TOKENS tokens, like vLLM's
457|    token budget, and only the last position is scored, as in mlx_lm generate:
458|    scoring all 32 x 1,024 positions at once needs 8.4 GB of logits.
459|    """
460|    chunk = max(1, PREFILL_TOKENS // ids.shape[0])
461|    end = ids.shape[1] - 1
462|    for i in range(0, end, chunk):
463|        model(ids[:, i : min(i + chunk, end)], cache=cache)
464|        mx.eval([c.state for c in cache])
465|    return greedy(model(ids[:, -1:], cache=cache))

468|def run_plain(model, rows, prompt, tokens, seed):
469|    mx.clear_cache()  # the previous run's buffers
470|    mx.random.seed(seed)
471|    cache = make_prompt_cache(model)
472|    y = prefill(model, mx.random.randint(0, 100000, (rows, prompt)), cache)
473|    mx.eval(y)
474|    for _ in range(tokens - 1):
475|        REC.begin_step(t=time.perf_counter(), rows=rows, prefill=0)
476|        REC.meta["ctx"] = rows * cache[0].offset
477|        REC.maybe_census(rows, 0)
478|        logits = REC.call("target_forward", model, (y,), {"cache": cache})
479|        ny = REC.call("sampling", greedy, (logits,), {})
480|        REC.call("submit", mx.async_eval, (ny,), {})
481|        REC.call("wait_gpu", to_list, (y,), {})
482|        y = ny
483|    REC.end_step()
484|    y.tolist()

5|# From round 3, an improvement must hold in both phases, decode and prefill, and an attempt may hand prefill-sized inputs to the compiled reference
6|
7|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*
8|
9|**The change.** Claude's comparison of every engine version over whole requests ([findings](../findings/muse-round-2.md), section 5) found that the grader and G3 timed only the decode step. They never timed the prefill, the phase in which a request's whole prompt runs through the model:
10|- **Experts attempt-7** looked like round 2's largest gain, a 19% shorter decode step at 32 requests. It processed prompts 6.6 to 14.5 times slower and cut throughput by 10% to 83%.
11|- **Routing attempt-4,** round 2's only baseline, processed prompts 7% to 10% slower. At 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts it cost 3.5% of throughput.
12|
13|The Muse agent never saw either effect: its piece timing ran decode sizes only, and G3 measured the decode step only.
14|
15|On 2026-11-04 surucuonur set the rule: "The improvement should be in the two phases of it: decode and prefill. Then, we can consider it as an improvement." surucuonur chose:
16|- **faster in one phase, slower in neither;**
17|- **the hand-off:** an attempt may leave prefill-sized inputs to the compiled reference. This replaces the part of [ADR 0010](0010-exact-at-every-size.md) that required the kernels to run in every call.
18|
19|## How it works
20|
21|- **The piece timing runs at the six G2 sizes** (`bench/grader/check_candidate.py`): decode at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and the first prefill chunk at 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. The layers are still chained.
22|- **The verdict at each size comes from paired repeats.** The candidate and the compiled reference run in alternating order, 30 times, and so does the baseline when one is given.
23|  - The candidate is `faster` when it wins at least 22 of the 30 pairs, a one-sided sign test at p < 0.01.
24|  - It is `slower` when it loses at least 22, and `same` otherwise.
25|
26|  This replaces the comparison of medians for the decode sizes too, since the same kernel timed twice differs by up to 5%.
27|- **The verdict per phase:**
28|  - a phase is `faster` when every one of its sizes is;
29|  - it is `slower` when any size is;
30|  - otherwise it is `not slower`.
31|
32|  `beats_compiled`, and `beats_baseline` against a baseline, are true when one phase is `faster` and neither is `slower`.
33|- **The hand-off** (`max_rows` in `spec.json`, `bench/grader/slots.py`). Inputs with more rows than `max_rows` run the slot's reference under `mx.compile`. G2 still checks every size.
34|  - On 2026-11-04 the compiled reference of each slot was bit-exact with the reference at all six sizes (`bench/micro/compiled_exact.py`, `results/runs/2026-11-04-handoff-check/`).
35|  - Above `max_rows` a hand-off runs the compiled reference itself, so it times `same` as the bar there, never better.
36|- **G3** (`bench/grader/time_candidates.py`, which writes `g3-vllm.json`):
37|  - **Workloads:** 1, 8 and 32 requests with 128-token prompts, and 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts.
38|  - **Measurements per run:** the decode step period, the prompt time and the whole-request time, over 5 shuffled repeats, up from 3.
39|  - **Faster and slower:** the two ranges over the repeats don't overlap.
40|  - **Why 5 repeats:** with 3 each, two identical engines' ranges miss each other by chance 1 time in 20 per direction. "Never slower" checks a phase 8 times (4 workloads, 2 bars), so a phase that changed nothing would fail about a third of the time. The first run under these rules showed it. A copy of experts attempt-7 with a hand-off at 59 rows came out `slower` on prompt time at 32 × 1,024, by 0.5% with ranges 16 ms apart, although above 59 rows it runs the compiled reference, whose own range overlapped the unchanged engine's (`results/runs/2026-11-04-handoff-check/`). With 5 repeats the chance is 1 in 252 per check, about 3% over 8.
41|  - **The pass rule:** against both the original model and the compiled reference, the decode step or the prompt time must be faster in every workload, neither may be slower in any, and no whole request may be slower.
42|- **The unchanged engine is vLLM's own.** The original model in G3 runs with Claude's step hooks, and with vLLM's engine inside the script's process. On 2026-11-04, alternating runs found it within −0.2% to +1.9% of vLLM with neither, inside the spread between repeats in every workload (`bench/micro/clean_vllm.py`, `results/runs/2026-11-04-clean-vllm/`).
43|
44|## Consequences
45|
46|- **Round 3 starts with no baseline.** Routing attempt-4 is `slower` at all three prefill sizes, 2.6 to 8.7 times the compiled reference's time. It fails G3 on prompt time at 8 and 32 requests. It becomes a starting point, so round 3's bar in every slot is the compiled reference.
47|- **A decode kernel no longer has to win at prefill sizes,** only to hand them off or not lose there. The attempt chooses the row count, so the boundary agent checks that the hand-off sits on the right side of 60 rows for the experts slot.
48|- **At prefill sizes, a slot with a hand-off is MLX's code, not the Muse agent's.** The claim for such an attempt is "faster decode, unchanged prefill".
49|- **Grader runs and G3 take longer.** Every attempt is now timed at three more sizes. G3 runs 5 repeats instead of 3, and its 32 × 1,024 workload adds at least 16 s per variant per repeat.
50|- **The decode verdict is stricter.** An attempt whose median beat the compiled reference by noise is now `same`.
51|- **Not covered:** prefill chunks of other sizes, and decode steps with other row counts. The boundary agent reports them; G3's four workloads are the end-to-end check.
52|- **At 1 request the whole-request time is noisy.** On 2026-11-04 its repeats spread 6% to 41%, so G3 there mostly says `same`, which passes the "never slower" test without showing a gain.
53|
54|## Considered options
55|
56|- **Faster in both phases.** The higher bar. A decode kernel would also have to beat MLX's large matrix kernels at 2,048 rows, which is not where the decode step loses its time. Not chosen.
57|- **Whole-request throughput alone.** Simple, but it lets a slower phase be traded for a faster one. surucuonur ruled that out.
58|- **Hand off to the uncompiled reference.** The prefill could then come out `slower` than the compiled reference wherever compiling helps; at 127 rows, routing's compiled reference takes 87 µs per layer against 102 µs uncompiled.
59|- **Keep the kernels in every call** (ADR 0010). The kernels could still branch on the row count inside themselves, but they couldn't use MLX's large-size kernels. surucuonur chose the hand-off.

5|# From round 2, a kernel must be bit-exact at every size it runs at, prefill included, and the piece timing chains the layers
6|
7|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*
8|
9|*[ADR 0011](0011-decode-and-prefill.md) changes two parts of this record on 2026-11-04, before round 3. An attempt may hand inputs above a row count it chooses to the compiled reference, instead of running its kernels in every call. The piece timing and G3 also time the prefill. Bit-exactness at every size and the chained timing stand.*
10|
11|**The change.** Claude's measurement of round 1 ([findings](../findings/muse-round-1.md)) found that round 1's final attempts, which passed the grader, broke the brief's end-to-end rule in the model, and that one of them slowed the decode step it was meant to speed up. The grader missed three things:
12|
13|1. **Sizes.** It tested a slot on a decode step's inputs only, at 1, 8 and 32 rows. The same `MoE.__call__` runs the prefill, at 127 to 2,048 rows with 128-token prompts. From 60 rows on, MLX's own experts kernel changes, from `gather_qvm` to `gather_qmm_rhs`, and so does its rounding. Round 1's experts kernel copied `gather_qvm` bit for bit, and differed in 62% of its outputs at each prefill size.
14|2. **Exactness.** G2 allowed small differences: 2 bfloat16 units in the last place, and 10⁻⁴ for routing weights. End to end, the brief asks for the same greedy tokens, and greedy decoding turns any difference into different tokens. Round 1's routing weights, within 10⁻⁵ of the reference, changed 7 to 9 of 32 sequences in 24 tokens.
15|3. **Latency.** The piece timing ran 20 layers' calls with no data between them, so the GPU could overlap them. At 1 row, round 1's experts kernel was 29% faster than the reference on overlapped calls and 66% slower on chained ones (`bench/micro/chain_timing.py`). In the model it slowed the decode step by 1.2 ms (22% in vLLM, 25% in plain MLX).
16|
17|On 2026-11-04 surucuonur chose, before round 2:
18|- **every call:** the kernels run wherever `MoE.__call__` runs, the prefill included;
19|- **bit-exact** outputs;
20|- **chained** piece timing.
21|
22|## How it works
23|
24|- **G2 at two kinds of size.** `bench/grader/check_candidate.py` checks every layer at:
25|  - the captured decode inputs, at 1, 8 and 32 rows;
26|  - the first prefill chunk at 1, 8 and 32 requests (127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows), recorded while it runs (`slots.capture_prefill`), with the prompts `time_candidates.py` uses.
27|- **Bit-exact.** An output passes only if it equals the reference's:
28|  - for routing, the 4 experts and their weights, in the same order, since combine sums the pairs in that order;
29|  - for combine and experts, every element.
30|
31|  The grader still reports the largest gap, in units in the last place, to help find the cause. The reference checked against itself shows no difference at any size.
32|- **Chained timing.** Each layer's call takes one input through `link`, a single fused kernel that adds 0 × one value of the previous call's output, so the call can't start before the previous one finishes. Every function timed (reference, compiled, candidate and baseline) gets the same link. The chained times match those of a real data chain within 10%.
33|  - **Why not `mx.depends`:** it orders only the graph. In a test on 2026-11-04, round 1's experts kernel took 46 µs per layer with it at 1 row, as fast as with no dependency, against 133 to 195 µs with a real data dependency in three runs.
34|- **The end-to-end check and G3 are unchanged.**
35|  - `bench/grader/time_candidates.py` now takes several `SLOT=FOLDER` attempts.
36|  - It times each slot alone, against its own compiled reference, and all of them together.
37|
38|## Consequences
39|
40|- **No round-1 attempt passes the new G2,** so round 2 has no baseline in any slot. Its bar is the compiled reference. Round 1's final attempts are its starting points, named in Claude's findings.
41|- **The experts slot needs a kernel exact at prefill sizes,** matching `gather_qmm_rhs`'s rounding from 60 rows on, or a single design whose rounding matches both of MLX's kernels.
42|- **A grader run takes longer.** It loads the model (760 MB) for every slot and runs three prefill chunks.
43|- **The piece timing now includes one small link kernel per layer** for every function timed. That brings the reference and the candidate closer in relative terms, but not in µs.
44|- **Not covered:** prefill speed. G3 times decode steps only, so a kernel slower at prefill sizes would go unnoticed, apart from the time to first token.
45|
46|## Considered options
47|
48|- **Decode calls only,** with MLX's code in the prefill. The kernels would need to be exact only at decode sizes, but they would no longer replace the whole MoE block. Not chosen: surucuonur asked for every call.
49|- **Keep the tolerances, and relax the token rule** to counting the sequences that differ. Simpler kernels, but the claim would become "the same model up to rounding", with a threshold to pick.
50|- **Keep independent timing,** and rely on G3 to catch latency. Round 2's builders would again rank attempts by a number that hid a 22% slowdown.
51|- **`mx.depends` for the chain.** No extra kernel, but it doesn't make the GPU wait.

74|## What building taught
75|
76|The analysis corrected by what the attempts showed (see `../implementation/README.md`):
77|
78|1. **Fusion beats grouping in the experts slot.** The ranking put the grouped-read ideal first ([ineff-quantized-kernels-1.md](ineff-quantized-kernels-1.md), 8.6 ms at 32 rows), but the grouped designs lost: attempt-1 (full fused grouped, 15 versions) and attempt-3 (grouped two-kernel) beat compiled only at 32 rows, while attempt-2/4's per-pair fusion won at 1+8 rows and tied at 32. Grouping overhead (pair scan, chunking, barriers, phantom work; duty-cycle ceiling ~55 GB/s vs the 150 ideal) eats the byte savings in the piece harness. The realizable prize came from launch fusion + occupancy + memory-level parallelism, not from reading each expert once.
79|2. **The piece harness prices kernels differently from in-step knock-outs.** A fused kernel costs a ~24 µs/layer floor with barriers/serial tails (routing) and ~17 µs/layer streaming elementwise (combine) — not 6.81 µs per launch; the reference's 12 routing kernels cost ~3 µs each when pipelined 20 deep. Future predictions must use harness floors; G3 decides the in-step truth.
80|3. **Experts G2 numerics key** (for the next round's builders): MLX's compiled swiglu computes entirely in bf16 — replicate per-op rounding or fail G2 at ~7%; gate/up/hidden must match bitwise (qvm strided-lane + `simd_sum` order) because down outputs near cancellation amplify 1-ULP flips; the stable bfloat sigmoid is replicable bit-exactly. Start from attempt-4's inner loop.
81|4. **1-row piece baselines shift between runs** (experts eager 64–100, compiled 62–135 µs/layer across runs on the same machine) — cross-run absolute comparisons are unreliable; within-run vs-compiled is the valid comparison, and G3's spread check matters most at 1 row. The 8/32-row baselines are stable.
82|5. **Combine's 2-ULP touch is safe**: it is FMA contraction, max exactly 2.0 on realistic inputs with zero exceedances over 20M resampled elements; only adversarial `shared ≈ −acc` cancellation exceeds it. The G2-margin worry was theoretical.

97|A decode step produces one token per request. On plain MLX with 128-token prompts the bare step takes 4.75 / 13.37 / 28.19 ms at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (Claude: `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md`, via round 1); in vLLM the unchanged step Claude re-measured for round 1 takes 5.370 / 14.363 / 29.851 ms (`claude/findings/muse-round-1.md` §3). A step is 867 kernels at 1 row, 987 at 32 rows, far below both hardware limits (whole-step 24–41 GB/s against 200 GB/s peak, ≤9% of peak compute), so it is overhead-bound throughout. Each tiny kernel costs ~6.81 µs end to end in the whole-step accounting, but the piece harness prices kernels differently (see *Territory map*): a fused kernel's floor is ~17 µs per layer when barrier-free and ~24 µs with barriers/serial tails, while the reference's kernels cost ~3–4.5 µs each when pipelined 20 deep. Round 2 ranks by the chained piece timing (each layer's call waits for the previous through the grader's `link` kernel), which matches the model's real dependency; the old independent timing is retained only as history.

Per layer it launches: routing, 12 kernels (router cast+matmul+sigmoid, bias add, negate, argpartition, gather, weight norm); the routed experts, 7 kernels at 1 row (3 products + activation + 3 off-chain index ranges) and 13 from 16 rows (6 sort/unsort glue kernels); combine, 5 kernels (cast, multiply, sum, cast, add with the shared expert); plus the shared expert, 4 kernels. The three slots mirror this split: `routing` (240 kernels/step), `experts` (140–260/step), `combine` (100/step). At 1 row, routing costs 1.02 ms and combine 0.61 ms — together 1.63 ms of the 4.75 ms step (34%), more than the routed experts' 0.92 ms. At 32 rows the experts cost 14.67 ms of 28.19 ms (52%) while routing falls to 1.68 ms (6%) and combine to 0.33 ms (1%). The experts read 908 MB at 32 rows against 443 MB for the distinct experts — half the bytes are repeat reads, and even so the path runs at only 62 GB/s (31% of peak), so most of it is kernel efficiency, not bytes. Those costs are Claude's knock-outs and counters; the mechanisms are the swarm's readings, round 1's carried forward where they still hold and this round's where the starting points changed the code in the slot.

156|## What building taught
157|
158|The analysis corrected by what the attempts showed (see `../implementation/README.md`):
159|
160|1. **Scalar sums reproduce MMA rounding — the round's central surprise.** Exploration held that the steel regimes' 8-product hardware accumulation could not be reproduced by scalar reordering (`ineff-baseline-routing-1`). Routing attempt-2 disproved it at decode sizes and attempt-3 at all six: serial scalar sums over the same partition/K order are bit-identical to `simdgroup_float8x8` accumulation on this GPU, including the 8-partition (127-row) and single-accumulator (>768) groupings. The same held for experts prefill: attempt-1's serial BK=32 scalar path matched `gather_qmm_rhs` bit for bit, as did attempt-2's MMA-tile form. Future exact kernels should try scalar first — it is simpler and, once staged, faster.
161|2. **Unstaged scalar is latency-bound; staging is the fix, not MMA.** Routing attempt-3 (scalar, device loads) ran 300 µs/layer at 8/32 rows on uncoalesced loads and threadgroup bank conflicts; attempt-4 (same sums, coalesced `float4` staging, padded `x`) runs 69–73 µs and beats compiled everywhere. The barrier count (24/row) did not bind; cross-threadgroup overlap hides it.
162|3. **Experts 1-row latency is a plateau, not a packing problem.** Six G2-exact attempts spanning 4 to 144 threadgroups per call, 128–512 threads per group, fused and split, interleaved and parallel-stored, all chain at 92–110 µs/layer at 1 row against compiled 73–87. Width, group count, interleave and store parallelism each moved 8/32 rows (best 510 µs at 32 rows, attempt-7) and none moved 1 row by more than ~12 µs. The remainder is the per-block serial K chains plus chained fixed cost; a fused exact kernel may need to stop fusing (reference-shaped separate products) to win at 1 row — untested, since every attempt kept at most two kernels.
163|4. **Chained floors replace independent floors.** Combine's ~17 µs independent floor is ~32–40 µs chained; routing's compiled bar is 56–91 µs chained against 30–49 independent. Every builder prediction anchored on the independent basis missed by +80–150% in the same direction, candidates and compiled alike. Predict only on the chained basis; within-run vs-compiled remains the valid comparison (1-row baselines still shift 73–87 µs for experts across runs).
164|5. **Contraction suppression needs volatile, not `precise`.** The literal `precise float` qualifier does not compile under MLX 0.32.4's header; `volatile` thread-local round-trips reproduce the reference's per-op roundings exactly (differ 0 over 49.6M graded combine elements) in both combine organizations. The residual is toolchain dependence — re-grade after any MLX/macOS change (boundary-3).

339|## Decision
340|
341|Best: `muse-spark/kernels/experts/attempt-4` (builder-1-d: attempt-2 hardened to 256 threads/pair). Why: passes G1, G2 bit-exact (max_ulp 0.0 at all rows) and its boundary check; beats BOTH eager and compiled at all three row counts (50.0 / 157.8 / 515.4 vs eager 64.3 / 218.6 / 765.7 vs compiled 65.3 / 217.4 / 760.2 µs/layer); fastest of the four attempts at every row count. Attempt-2 is second (beats compiled everywhere, but regressed 7.5% vs eager at 1 row before the occupancy fix). The grouped designs lost: attempt-1 (full fused grouped, 15 versions) and attempt-3 (grouped 2-kernel) win only at 32 rows — grouping's byte savings don't convert in the piece harness (duty-cycle ceiling ~55 GB/s vs the 150 ideal; scan/chunk/barrier overhead exceeds the traffic saved). Fusion without grouping captured the harness prize. No further hardening: builder-1-d names no further single change (512 threads/group is a ≤10% gamble against real regression risk); the only remaining direction is cross-pair grouping, a different change class that three directions showed loses in-harness. G3 should show: a faster step at all three concurrencies. Piece basis predicts −0.29 / −1.22 / −5.01 ms/step ((64.3−50.0), (218.6−157.8), (765.7−515.4) µs/layer × 20 layers); the knock-out bases span −0.40/−1.30/−3.67 ms (measured grouped) to −0.5/−2.5/−8.6 ms (ideal streaming). Caveat: 1-row harness baselines shift between runs (64.3/65.3 here vs 99.8/135.0 in attempt-2's run), so the 1-row margin needs G3's spread check; 8/32-row baselines are stable across runs.

1|# Attempt 1 — builder-3-a, direction (a): thread-per-output + precise stepwise sum
2|
3|First attempt in this direction (round 2, `hyp-3-combine-exact`, slot
4|`combine`, baseline `none`). Builds on the starting point
5|`muse-spark/kernels/combine/attempt-1` (`block-0.metal:12-25`,
6|`spec.json`: grid `rows*768`, threadgroup [256,1,1], no threadgroup
7|memory). The starting point is not a baseline: under round 2's bit-exact
8|G2 it fails at five of six sizes on FMA contraction alone (decode
9|0 / 2 / 2 differ, prefill 6 / 50 / 130; `ineff-baseline-combine-1`,
10|`territory-baseline-combine.md` checklist D), so it counts as the attempt
11|this one changes.
12|
13|## What changed
14|
15|Only the arithmetic. Indexing, grid, threadgroup, inputs/outputs and the
16|final line `bfloat(acc) + shared[sbase]` are verbatim from the starting
17|point. The single-expression sum
18|
19|```metal
20|float acc = float(y0)*w0 + float(y1)*w1 + float(y2)*w2 + float(y3)*w3;
21|```
22|
23|which the compiler FP-contracts into FMAs (each product kept unrounded
24|into its add), becomes seven fma-free stepwise ops with explicit
25|rounding barriers:
26|
27|```metal
28|volatile float p0 = float(y[ybase]) * weights[wbase];        // rounded to f32
29|volatile float p1 = float(y[ybase+768u]) * weights[wbase+1u];
30|volatile float p2 = float(y[ybase+1536u]) * weights[wbase+2u];
31|volatile float p3 = float(y[ybase+2304u]) * weights[wbase+3u];
32|volatile float s01 = p0 + p1;                                // rounded to f32
33|volatile float s012 = s01 + p2;                              // rounded to f32
34|volatile float acc = s012 + p3;                              // rounded to f32
35|out[sbase] = bfloat(acc) + shared[sbase];                    // verbatim
36|```
37|
38|Each `volatile` store materialises its f32 value, so no product can stay
39|unrounded into the next add and no add can be fused with a later mul;
40|the fold is exactly `((p0+p1)+p2)+p3` with a rounding after every add,
41|then one bfloat16 round and the single-rounding bfloat16 `+ shared`,
42|matching the reference's separate kernels (`binary_g` multiply,
43|`col_reduce_small` sum, `copy_v`, `binary_vv`; `slots.py:51-52`,
44|Boundary steps 1–5). No reassociation, no `fma`, no threadgroup memory.
45|
46|Note on spelling: the literal `precise float` qualifier does not compile
47|under MLX 0.32.4 (`metal::precise` is a function namespace in the MLX
48|header, e.g. `metal::precise::exp`; a leading `precise` is parsed as
49|that namespace and rejected). Volatile stepwise barriers are the
50|"explicit rounding barriers" the hypothesis design names as the
51|alternative to `metal::precise` operations, with the same semantics:
52|every mul rounds once to f32, every add rounds once to f32. Probes
53|outside the grader (random [512,4,768] inputs vs the eager MLX
54|reference, 3 × 393,216 elements) gave differ 3–4 for the starting
55|point's contracted expression and differ 0 for this kernel.
56|

2|
3|Hardening attempt for `hyp-1-experts-exact` (slot `experts`, baseline
4|`none`). Builds on the best attempt
5|`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-1` (G2 pass all six,

9|constraint.

11|## The one main change
12|
13|Split attempt-1's single fused per-pair kernel (4 threadgroups per
14|call at 1 row, 512 threads each) into two kernels with 4-block
15|threadgroups, exposing more threadgroups per call without
16|attempt-2's 1-simdgroup-per-group collapse:
17|
18|- `experts_gate_up` (block-0): one 128-thread threadgroup (4
19|  simdgroups) owns 4 distinct 32-output blocks — simdgroup `s` of
20|  chunk `c = tg % 3` computes block `blk = c*4 + s` of pair
21|  `tg / 3` (12 blocks/pair ÷ 4 = 3 groups/pair). Grid
22|  `rows*1536` threads = `rows*12` groups: **12 groups at 1 row**
23|  (96 at 8, 384 at 32). Each simdgroup runs gate then up for its
24|  block, lane 0 (decode) or every lane (prefill) stores the
25|  bfloat16-rounded results to `tg_gate`/`tg_up`, one barrier, then
26|  every lane applies the shared full-bfloat16 silu-mul and writes
27|  `hidden[pair, blk*32 + lane]`.
28|- `experts_down` (block-1): same shape for the 24 down blocks —
29|  `blk = (tg % 6)*4 + simd`, pair `tg / 6` (24 ÷ 4 = 6 groups/pair).
30|  Grid `rows*3072` threads = `rows*24` groups: **24 groups at
31|  1 row** (192 at 8, 768 at 32).
32|
33|Everything else is copied, not redesigned:
34|
35|- **Decode (`rows < 60`):** `qvm_block` in block-2 is byte-identical
36|  to attempt-1's (verified by diff; itself attempt-4's proven
37|  helper) — strided lanes `k ≡ lane (mod 32)` serial in float32,
38|  float32 dequant `x·(scale·q+bias)`, `simd_sum` tree. Splitting
39|  blocks across threadgroups does not change any block's
40|  accumulation order, so decode bits are attempt-1's.
41|- **Prefill (`rows >= 60`):** `qmm_accum` in block-2 is
42|  byte-identical to attempt-1's scalar path (verified by diff) —
43|  weight rounded to bfloat16 first
44|  (`float(bfloat(scale·q+bias))`), then K accumulated contiguously
45|  in `BK=32` tile order by one thread per output, one output per
46|  lane. Attempt-2's MMA tiles (`qmm_block`,
47|  `simdgroup_multiply_accumulate`, 6,144 B of float tile buffers)
48|  are **not** used, so no tile memory is allocated in either branch
49|  and decode residency is not taxed for prefill.
50|- Same branch threshold (`rows >= 60` from `inds_shape[0]`, the
51|  `gather_qmm_rhs` dispatch threshold, not the tested sizes), same
52|  four bfloat16 rounding points (gate, up, hidden via silu-mul,
53|  down — silu helper byte-identical to attempt-2's copy of
54|  attempt-4's full-bfloat16 lowering), fp32 accumulation, and

56|  indexed by the same flat pair).

61|  leaves 12 of 16 GPU cores idle per call (4 threadgroups). Here a
62|  1-row layer call exposes 12 (gate/up) then 24 (down)
63|  threadgroups, so up to 12/16 cores hold gate/up work and all 16
64|  hold down work, while each group keeps 4 blocks in flight —
65|  the in-group load overlap whose loss (1 block/group) cost
66|  attempt-2 its 8/32-row wins (326.8/887.6). Cost of the split:

79|## Limits (by hand; the grader does not check the 32 KB cap)
80|
81|128 threads/group ≤ 1,024. Threadgroup memory: gate/up
82|`tg_x[768] + tg_gate[128] + tg_up[128]` bfloat16 = **2,048 B**;

90|

127|mapping moved), and prefill reuses attempt-1's `qmm_accum`

130|## Verdict
131|
132|G1 pass; **G2 pass at all six sizes, differ 0 / max_ulp 0.0
133|everywhere** (decode 1/8/32 and prefill 127/1,016/2,048) — the
134|split kept attempt-1's bits in both regimes: per-block
135|`qvm_block` order unchanged by the block→group remapping, and the
136|scalar `qmm_accum` prefill path matched `gather_qmm_rhs` again.
137|Chained timing µs/layer (this run; candidate vs reference vs
138|compiled): **1 row 109.5 / 93.1 / 86.9 (loses both)**; 8 rows
139|195.0 / 248.8 / 243.6 (wins); 32 rows 637.7 / 846.0 / 798.9
140|(wins). `beats_compiled` false — the 1-row size still misses, as
141|in attempt-1. Baseline `none` — no
142|`wins_vs_baseline`/`beats_baseline`.
143|
144|Against attempt-1 (different run; 1-row baselines shifted
145|77.6 → 86.9 compiled between runs, so treat 1 row as indicative):
146|109.5 vs 104.3 at 1 row (no gain), 195.0 vs 193.3 at 8 rows
147|(flat), 637.7 vs 535.7 at 32 rows (**+19% regression**). The
148|hardening did not beat the best attempt at any size.
149|
150|## Miss analysis (prediction 74 / 162 / 530; all misses > 20%)
151|
152|Measured 109.5 / 195.0 / 637.7 is **+48% / +20% / +20%** over
153|prediction. Effective bandwidth on pair bytes: 20 / 91 / 111 GB/s
154|— the 1- and 8-row rates are attempt-1's (21 / 92 GB/s), and the
155|32-row rate falls between attempt-2's 80 and attempt-1's 132 GB/s.
156|Three facts together locate the error in the prediction's model,
157|not in the arithmetic:
158|
159|1. **Group count is not the 1-row binding limit past 4 groups.**
160|   Attempt-1 (4 groups × 512 threads), attempt-2 (48+96 groups ×
161|   32 threads) and this attempt (12+24 groups × 128 threads, 4
162|   blocks in flight per group, 2,048/768 B threadgroup memory) all
163|   land at 103.6–109.5 µs/layer chained at 1 row, across a 36×
164|   range of group counts. The prediction assumed attempt-1's
165|   serial part scales with cores busy (4 → 12); instead the
166|   ~100 µs plateau is invariant to how the blocks are packed. What
167|   does not shrink under any packing is each block's own serial
168|   K chain (24 strided load-accumulate steps per lane for gate,
169|   24 for up, 12 for down, gate→up→down ordered by the hidden
170|   dependency) plus the chained launch/link fixed cost — and this
171|   attempt *adds* a second launch and a `hidden` round-trip on
172|   that chain. Splitting exposes cores the critical path cannot
173|   use.
174|2. **At 32 rows the split tax is real and the fused kernel's
175|   in-group overlap was load-bearing.** 637.7 vs attempt-1's
176|   535.7: the two-kernel form pays 1,152 group dispatches (vs
177|   128), 3× duplicated `tg_x` loads and 6× duplicated `tg_h`
178|   loads, two extra barrier rounds per pair, and the `hidden`
179|   write+read — small bytes (<1% of weight traffic) but pure
180|   latency/occupancy overhead at streaming sizes, while a fused
181|   512-thread group keeps 16 blocks' loads in flight behind one
182|   barrier set. Restoring 4 blocks/group and low threadgroup
183|   memory recovered most of attempt-2's loss (80 → 111 GB/s) but
184|   not attempt-1's 132 GB/s.
185|3. **The 8-row rate confirms the mechanism:** 91 GB/s equals
186|   attempt-1's 92 GB/s — once enough groups exist to stream, the
187|   packing makes no difference, and the prediction's assumed
188|   residency gain (115 GB/s from lower threadgroup memory) did
189|   not appear; residency was not the cap.
190|
191|Lesson for `ineff-baseline-experts-2`: the 1-row lever is not
192|threadgroups per call (three packings, one plateau). The next
193|lever must shorten or overlap the per-block serial chain itself
194|— e.g. interleaving the independent gate and up K-loops so one's
195|loads hide the other's latency — or cut the chained fixed cost,
196|without touching any block's `simd_sum` order.
197|
198|**Next change (one):** return to attempt-1's fused single kernel
199|and interleave gate/up: issue both blocks' K-loop loads per wave
200|before accumulating, keeping `qvm_block`'s per-block order and
201|all rounding points identical.

20|branch only:
21|
22|- **Before (attempt-1):** simdgroup `b` (`b < 12`) ran
23|  `qvm_block(gate, block b)` to completion (24 strided K steps per
24|  lane: `k = lane, lane+32, ..., lane+744`; each step loads 4 weight
25|  words + scale/bias for that `k`, then accumulates 32 outputs),
26|  stored `tg_gate`, then ran `qvm_block(up, block b)` the same way
27|  and stored `tg_up`. The two blocks' K loops were fully sequential:
28|  up's first load waited for gate's last accumulate.
29|- **Now:** simdgroup `b` runs one merged loop,
30|  `qvm_gate_up_pair` (block-1). For each strided `k`, both blocks'
31|  loads are issued first — gate's 4 weight words, scale and bias,
32|  then up's 4 weight words, scale and bias (plus the shared
33|  `tg_x[k]`, read once) — and only then do the two accumulation
34|  passes run, gate's 32 terms then up's 32 terms, into separate
35|  accumulators `pg`/`pu`. The next `k`'s loads therefore sit behind
36|  twice the issued load traffic per step, and each block's load
37|  latency has the other block's loads/compute to hide behind
38|  (double-buffering the two blocks' weight/scale/x loads within
39|  the step). Lane 0 then stores both blocks in one loop:
40|  `tg_gate[b*32+j] = (bfloat)pg[j]`, `tg_up[b*32+j] = (bfloat)pu[j]`.
41|
42|Everything else is copied, not redesigned:
43|
44|- **Per-block bits unchanged.** In `qvm_gate_up_pair`, each block's
45|  adds run in exactly `qvm_block`'s order: the same strided `k`
46|  sequence, the same float32 dequant terms
47|  `x * (s0 * (by & 0x0f) + bias)` /
48|  `x * (s1 * (by & 0xf0) + bias)` with `s1 = scale/16`, in the same
49|  per-output sequence; `pg` and `pu` are independent accumulators,
50|  so interleaving the two blocks cannot reorder either block's own
51|  adds. Each accumulator then gets the identical
52|  `#pragma clang loop unroll(full)` `simd_sum` tree as `qvm_block`.
53|  Down still calls `qvm_block` verbatim (verified by diff against
54|  attempt-1: `qvm_block` and `qmm_accum` bodies byte-identical;
55|  block-0 differs only in the header comment and the decode
56|  gate/up call site).
57|- **Prefill (`rows >= 60`) unchanged.** Attempt-1's scalar
58|  `qmm_accum` (weight rounded to bfloat16 first,
59|  `float(bfloat(scale·q+bias))`, then K accumulated contiguously in
60|  `BK=32` tile order, one output per lane) is copied byte-identical
61|  for gate, up and down, and block-0's prefill branch is untouched —
62|  the interleaving does not touch the prefill arithmetic.
63|- Same four bfloat16 rounding points (gate, up, hidden via the
64|  shared full-bfloat16 silu-mul, down — silu code byte-identical),
65|  fp32 accumulation, positional `y[r,j]` (`pair = r*4 + j`), and
66|  the same `rows >= 60` dispatch threshold from `x_shape[0]`, not
67|  the grader's bracketing sizes. No kernel split, no threadgroup
68|  count change, no new device-memory intermediate.

70|## Which inefficiency it removes, and how

74|  48+96 threadgroups per call, so the binding cost past 4 groups is
75|  each block's serial K chain (24 + 24 + 12 strided
76|  load-accumulate steps, gate→up→down ordered by the hidden
77|  dependency) executed with only one block's loads in flight per
78|  simdgroup at a time. Interleaving gate and up — the two
79|  independent, equal-length (24-step) chains — puts both blocks'
80|  loads in flight in every step without touching any block's
81|  `simd_sum` order, the only lever attempt-3's analysis left inside
82|  the fused kernel. Down (12 steps) is left sequential: it cannot
83|  start before the silu barrier in any case.

85|  attempt-1's branch; kept by reusing its scalar `qmm_accum`
86|  verbatim.

88|  kept, as in attempts 1–3 — weight bytes per pair stay
89|  552,960 B; the interleaving changes load scheduling, not bytes.

95|tg_gate[384] + tg_up[384] + tg_h[384]` bfloat16 = **3,840 B** of
96|32,768 B, rows-independent. The only new state is register-local:
97|a second 32-float accumulator `pu[32]` beside `p[32]` and a second

100|kernel is valid at every `rows ≥ 1`, on both sides of 60.

105|368,640 B = 2/3): 2.21 / 17.69 / 70.78 MB at 4 / 32 / 128 pairs.

136|## Verdict
137|
138|G1 pass; **G2 pass at all six sizes, differ 0 / max_ulp 0.0
139|everywhere** (decode 1/8/32 and prefill 127/1,016/2,048) — the
140|interleaving kept attempt-1's bits in both regimes: per-block
141|`qvm_block` add order unchanged by the within-step interleave, and
142|the byte-identical scalar `qmm_accum` prefill path matched
143|`gather_qmm_rhs` again. Chained timing µs/layer (this run;
144|candidate vs reference vs compiled): **1 row 94.0 / 81.2 / 73.5
145|(loses both)**; 8 rows 177.0 / 252.1 / 239.0 (wins); 32 rows
146|591.3 / 799.2 / 796.3 (wins). `beats_compiled` false — only the
147|1-row size misses, as in attempt-1. Baseline `none` — no
148|`wins_vs_baseline`/`beats_baseline`.
149|
150|Against attempt-1 (different run; compiled shifted 77.6 → 73.5
151|at 1 row between runs, so treat cross-run deltas as indicative):
152|94.0 vs 104.3 at 1 row (**−9.9%**), 177.0 vs 193.3 at 8 rows
153|(**−8.4%**), 591.3 vs 535.7 at 32 rows (**+10.4% regression**).
154|This is the first attempt to move below attempt-1's 103.6–109.5
155|µs/layer 1-row plateau (attempts 1–3) at any size, and it does so
156|at 1 and 8 rows — but it spends part of attempt-1's 32-row win.

158|## Miss analysis (prediction 90 / 178 / 505, measured 94.0 / 177.0 / 591.3)
159|
160|Misses are +4.4% / −0.6% / +17.1% — all inside the 20% bar, so no
161|formal miss, but the 32-row *direction* was wrong (predicted
162|−6% vs attempt-1, measured +10.4%), and that needs explaining:
163|
164|1. **The interleave works where latency binds.** Effective
165|   bandwidth on pair bytes: 23.5 GB/s at 1 row (attempt-1: 21.2)
166|   and 99.9 GB/s at 8 rows (attempt-1: 91.5). Doubling the loads
167|   outstanding per K step (8 weight words + two scale/bias pairs
168|   issued before either accumulation) hid enough of each block's
169|   load latency to break the 103.6–109.5 plateau that three
170|   threadgroup packings could not — confirming attempt-3's
171|   diagnosis that the per-block serial chain, not group count,
172|   was the 1-row lever. The gain is real but partial: 94.0 still
173|   loses to compiled 73.5, so roughly 20 µs/layer of the 1-row
174|   cost (chained launch/link, `tg_x` load, silu, barriers, down's
175|   still-sequential 12-step chain and its two waves) remains
176|   unoverlapped.
177|2. **At 32 rows the second accumulator is the tax.** 119.7 GB/s
178|   vs attempt-1's 132.1 GB/s. Once 128 groups saturate the GPU,
179|   exposed load latency is already hidden by group-level
180|   parallelism, so the interleave buys nothing — and its cost,
181|   a second live 32-float accumulator plus a second 4-word load
182|   buffer per thread for the whole K loop, is paid in register
183|   pressure and therefore resident-group occupancy on every
184|   streaming step. The prediction's assumed MLP lift to
185|   140 GB/s double-counted parallelism the group count already
186|   provided.
187|3. **The 8-row point separates the two regimes:** same register
188|   cost as 32 rows, but only 32 groups per call, so per-group
189|   load overlap still pays (91.5 → 99.9 GB/s, prediction exact).
190|   The crossover between "latency-bound, interleave wins" and
191|   "occupancy-bound, interleave taxes" sits between 8 and 32
192|   rows in this run.
193|
194|Lesson for `ineff-baseline-experts-2`: the serial-chain lever is
195|real (first sub-plateau 1-row result: 94.0), but a uniform
196|interleave trades it against streaming occupancy. The two
197|regimes want different code, and both arithmetics are
198|bit-identical, so the choice between them is free.
199|
200|**Next change (one):** make the interleave row-conditional
201|inside the same fused kernel — `qvm_gate_up_pair` below the
202|latency/occupancy crossover (e.g. `rows <= 8`), attempt-1's
203|sequential `qvm_block` gate then up above it — keeping the
204|1/8-row wins (94.0/177.0) while restoring attempt-1's 32-row
205|register profile (535.7). Both branches keep every block's
206|add order, so G2 is unaffected by where the crossover sits.

1|# attempt-5 (round 2): hardening — parallel block stores (builder-1-e)
2|
3|Hardening attempt for `hyp-1-experts-exact` (slot `experts`, baseline
4|`none`). Builds on `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-4`
5|(interleaved gate/up, fused single kernel, 512 threads/pair, G2 pass
6|all six, 94.0 / 177.0 / 591.3 µs/layer chained vs compiled
7|73.5 / 239.0 / 796.3 — loses only at 1 row).
8|
9|## The one main change
10|
11|Parallelize the block stores, decode branch only. Nothing else
12|changes: same `qvm_block` / `qvm_gate_up_pair` / `qmm_accum` bodies
13|(`block-1.metal` byte-identical to attempt-4, verified by diff),
14|same interleaved gate/up K loop, same silu, same prefill branch,
15|same grids and `spec.json` (byte-identical).
16|
17|- **Before (attempt-4):** after each block's `simd_sum`, lane 0 alone
18|  stored the block: `for (j = 0..31) tg_gate[b*32+j] = p[j]` and
19|  likewise `tg_up`, and for down `y[pair*768 + b*32 + j] = p[j]`.
20|  That is 48 blocks per pair (12 gate + 12 up + 24 down) × 32 serial
21|  stores, all on the 16 lanes-0 of the pair's threadgroup (12 active
22|  in gate/up, up to 16 per down wave), while the other 31 lanes of
23|  each simdgroup idle at the following barrier / next wave.
24|- **Now:** after each `simd_sum` every lane holds the full reduced
25|  32-vector (`p[j] = simd_sum(p[j])` for all `j` in `block-1.metal`,
26|  so each lane's `p[0..31]` is the whole block output). Lane `j`
27|  stores element `j` — one store per lane, 32-way parallel:
28|  `tg_gate[b*32 + lane] = (bfloat)p[lane]`,
29|  `tg_up[b*32 + lane] = (bfloat)pu[lane]`, and for down
30|  `y[pair*768 + b*32 + lane] = (bfloat)p[lane]` (still inside the
31|  `b < 24` guard, so idle simdgroups store nothing). The
32|  `(bfloat)` rounding at the store is unchanged, so the bfloat16
33|  rounding points are identical.
34|- **Prefill (`rows >= 60`) untouched:** it already stores one output
35|  per lane (`tg_gate[b*32 + lane]`, `y[... + lane]`), so there is no
36|  serial store to parallelize there.
37|
38|Correctness rests on `simd_sum` being a broadcast reduction: if any
39|lane held only its own partial, the parallel store would write
40|partials and G2 would fail loudly with large `differ` at decode
41|sizes. That is the intended check.
42|
43|## Which inefficiency it removes, and how
44|
45|- `ineff-baseline-experts-2` (chained 1-row latency): attempt-4's
46|  miss analysis left the still-sequential tails — chained fixed
47|  cost, `tg_x` load, silu, barriers and the down chain — plus these
48|  serial stores on the critical path. On the per-pair critical path
49|  the serial stores are: gate/up phase, 64 threadgroup stores by
50|  each active simdgroup's lane 0 (32 gate + 32 up, 12 simdgroups
51|  concurrent) before the silu barrier; down, 32 device stores per
52|  wave × 2 waves. That is ~128 serial store issues (plus their loop
53|  control) that every other lane waits on. Parallel stores cut that
54|  to 4 parallel store steps (gate 1, up 1, down 1 per wave),
55|  removing ~124 serial issues from the path without touching any
56|  accumulation order, so decode bits are attempt-4's by construction
57|  if the broadcast premise holds.
58|- `ineff-baseline-experts-1` (prefill G2 gate): already removed by
59|  attempt-4's branch; kept by reusing its scalar `qmm_accum`
60|  verbatim.
61|- `ineff-baseline-experts-3` (per-pair re-reads): deliberately
62|  kept, as in attempts 1–4 — weight bytes per pair stay 552,960 B;
63|  the store bytes are tiny beside them (`y` 1,536 B/pair = 0.28%).
64|
65|## Limits (by hand; the grader does not check the 32 KB cap)
66|
67|512 threads/group ≤ 1,024 and threadgroup memory unchanged at
68|3,840 B (`tg_x[768] + tg_gate[384] + tg_up[384] + tg_h[384]`
69|bfloat16) of 32,768 B, rows-independent (`spec.json` identical to
70|attempt-4). No new state: `p[lane]` reads the existing per-thread
71|accumulator. Valid at every `rows ≥ 1` on both sides of 60; decode
72|stores cover every `(pair, block, lane)` exactly once, as before
73|(gate/up: 12 simdgroups × 32 lanes; down: 24 blocks × 32 lanes over
74|2 waves).
75|
76|## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (chained, grader timing)
77|
78|Attempt-4 (other run): 94.0 / 177.0 / 591.3 vs compiled
79|73.5 / 239.0 / 796.3. Baseline `none`, so no
80|`wins_vs_baseline` / `beats_baseline`.
81|
82|- **1 row: 91.** Latency-bound. ~124 serial store issues leave the
83|  critical path; at ~20 exposed cycles each (single-lane store
84|  pipeline plus 32-iteration loop overhead, GPU ≈ 1.3 GHz) that is
85|  124 × 20 / 1.3e9 ≈ 1.9 µs, plus the down device stores' extra
86|  latency on lane 0, ≈ 3 µs total → 94.0 − 3 ≈ **91 µs**. Still
87|  above compiled 73.5 — this trims a tail, it does not close the
88|  remaining down-chain / fixed-cost gap.
89|- **8 rows: 175.** 32 groups per call partly hide one group's store
90|  tail behind other groups' K loops, so roughly half the 1-row
91|  saving survives: 177.0 − 2 ≈ **175 µs**, keeping the win over
92|  compiled 239.0.
93|- **32 rows: 589.** Streaming-bound (attempt-4: 119.7 GB/s on pair
94|  bytes). Store bytes are 0.28% of pair traffic and group-level
95|  parallelism already hides the store latency, so the change is
96|  ~neutral: 591.3 − 2 ≈ **589 µs**, keeping the win over compiled
97|  796.3. Risk: none structural — no register or threadgroup change;
98|  the only risk is the broadcast premise, which G2 tests directly.
99|
100|G2 prediction: pass at all six sizes with `differ == 0` — the
101|parallel store writes the same `(bfloat)p[j]` values attempt-4's
102|lane 0 wrote, just from lane `j` instead of lane 0, and the prefill
103|path is byte-identical to attempt-4's.
104|
105|## Verdict
106|
107|G1 pass; **G2 pass at all six sizes, differ 0 / max_ulp 0.0
108|everywhere** (decode 1/8/32 and prefill 127/1,016/2,048) — the
109|broadcast premise holds: every lane's `p[0..31]` after `simd_sum`
110|is the full reduced block, so lane `j` storing `p[j]` reproduces
111|attempt-4's serial lane-0 stores bit for bit, for gate, up and
112|down alike. Chained timing µs/layer (this run; candidate vs
113|reference vs compiled): **1 row 92.1 / 95.7 / 75.9 (loses to
114|compiled, beats reference)**; 8 rows 162.0 / 232.4 / 234.6 (wins);
115|32 rows 534.8 / 802.3 / 798.2 (wins). `beats_compiled` false —
116|only the 1-row size misses, as in attempt-4. Baseline `none` — no
117|`wins_vs_baseline`/`beats_baseline`.
118|
119|Against attempt-4 (different run; compiled shifted 73.5 → 75.9 at
120|1 row and reference 81.2 → 95.7 between runs, so treat cross-run
121|deltas as indicative): 92.1 vs 94.0 at 1 row (**−2.0%**), 162.0
122|vs 177.0 at 8 rows (**−8.5%**), 534.8 vs 591.3 at 32 rows
123|(**−9.6%**). Effective bandwidth on pair bytes: 24.0 / 109.2 /
124|132.3 GB/s (attempt-4: 23.5 / 99.9 / 119.7). The 32-row rate is
125|back at attempt-1's 132.1 GB/s level while keeping the
126|interleave's 1/8-row wins — attempt-5 dominates attempt-4 at
127|every size and matches the best previous 32-row time (attempt-1:
128|535.7).
129|
130|## Miss analysis (prediction 91 / 175 / 589, measured 92.1 / 162.0 / 534.8)
131|
132|Misses are +1.2% / −7.4% / −9.2% — all inside the 20% bar, so no
133|formal miss, but the size pattern was inverted versus the
134|prediction (smallest gain at 1 row, largest at 32 rows) and that
135|needs explaining:
136|
137|1. **At 1 row the serial stores were a small tail, as the
138|   arithmetic said, but the fixed remainder is larger than the
139|   store tail.** Removing ~124 serial issues bought only ~2 µs of
140|   the predicted ~3; the remaining ~16 µs gap to compiled (92.1 vs
141|   75.9) is the still-sequential down chain (12 strided steps × 2
142|   waves behind the silu barrier), the `tg_x` load, silu, barriers
143|   and the chained launch/link cost — none of which this change
144|   touches.
145|2. **At 8/32 rows the serial device stores cost more than pure
146|   latency.** Lane 0's 32 serial stores to `y` per down block are
147|   32 separate single-lane transactions to consecutive addresses;
148|   32 lanes storing in parallel coalesce into full transactions.
149|   Paid per block (24 per pair) on every streaming step, that
150|   inefficiency — plus the serial threadgroup stores delaying the
151|   silu barrier — taxed attempt-4 by ~9% at 32 rows, which the
152|   latency-only prediction (store bytes = 0.28% of pair traffic)
153|   missed. Parallel stores removed it, which is also why the
154|   interleave's 32-row register tax (attempt-4 notes) no longer
155|   shows: 534.8 ≈ attempt-1's non-interleaved 535.7.
156|
157|Lesson for `ineff-baseline-experts-2`: a serial lane-0 store
158|after a broadcast reduction is never free — at latency sizes it
159|is a barrier tail, at streaming sizes the uncoalesced device
160|stores tax every block. Any future block kernel should store
161|from all 32 lanes by default.
162|
163|## Next change
164|
165|Make the down product's two waves overlap like gate/up: one
166|simdgroup computes two down blocks in one interleaved K loop
167|(separate accumulators, per-block `qvm_block` order and the new
168|parallel store kept), attacking the still-sequential 12-step
169|down chain that is now the largest named remainder at 1 row.
170|The row-conditional interleave attempt-4 proposed is moot —
171|attempt-5 already restored attempt-1's 32-row rate (534.8 vs
172|535.7) with the interleave kept.

47|  distinct 32-float thread arrays — kernel-scope `p[32]`, a
48|  gate/up-scoped `pu[32]` and a down-scoped `q[32]` — and the
49|  compiler charged all three against the per-threadgroup budget
50|  (`maxTotalThreadsPerThreadgroup` 448 < 512) even though `pu` and
51|  `q` are live in disjoint phases. Attempt-7 hoists the second
52|  accumulator to kernel scope: `float p[32]; float q[32];` beside
53|  the existing buffers in `block-0`, and passes the same `q` as
54|  gate/up's second accumulator (`qvm_gate_up_pair(..., p, q)`) and
55|  as down's second accumulator (`qvm_down_pair(..., p, q)`),
56|  deleting both scoped declarations. The kernel again has two
57|  distinct 32-float thread arrays, exactly attempt-5's footprint,
58|  at unchanged 512 threads.
59|
60|Everything else is kept identical, as the task requires:
61|
62|- **Per-block bits unchanged.** In `qvm_down_pair` each block's adds
63|  run in exactly `qvm_block`'s order: the same strided `k` sequence,
64|  the same float32 dequant terms
65|  `x * (s0 * (by & 0x0f) + bias)` / `x * (s1 * (by & 0xf0) + bias)`
66|  with `s1 = scale/16`, in the same per-output sequence; the two
67|  accumulators are independent, so interleaving cannot reorder
68|  either block's own adds. Each accumulator then gets the identical
69|  `#pragma clang loop unroll(full)` `simd_sum` tree as `qvm_block`.
70|  The `(bfloat)` rounding at the store is unchanged.
71|- **Sharing is a pure storage rename.** Gate/up and down run in
72|  disjoint phases separated by two `threadgroup_barrier`s (after
73|  gate/up and after silu): gate/up's `q` values are stored to
74|  `tg_up` before the first barrier, silu consumes only
75|  `tg_gate`/`tg_up`/`tg_h`, and `qvm_down_pair` re-zeroes both
76|  `p[0..31]` and `q[0..31]` on entry (as `qvm_gate_up_pair` does),
77|  so no value can leak across the barrier through the shared array.
78|  Peak live floats per phase is unchanged (64 in gate/up, 64 in
79|  down); only the distinct-array count charged by the compiler
80|  drops from three to two.
81|- **Parallel lane stores kept.** After the two `simd_sum`s every
82|  lane holds both blocks' full reduced 32-vectors, so lane `j`
83|  stores element `j` of each block — one store per lane per block:
84|  `y[pair*768 + b0*32 + lane] = (bfloat)p[lane]`,
85|  `y[pair*768 + b1*32 + lane] = (bfloat)q[lane]`.
86|- **Gate/up interleave, silu, prefill scalar branch, grids and
87|  rounding points identical.** Gate/up still calls
88|  `qvm_gate_up_pair` with attempt-5's parallel `tg_gate`/`tg_up`
89|  stores; the full-bfloat16 silu-mul is byte-identical; the
90|  `rows >= 60` prefill branch still uses the scalar `qmm_accum`
91|  (bfloat16-rounded dequant, contiguous `BK=32` order) for gate,
92|  up and down, with the same `x_shape[0] >= 60` dispatch
93|  threshold; `spec.json` (one kernel, `rows*2048` threads =
94|  `rows*4` groups of 512) is byte-identical. No kernel split, no
95|  new device-memory intermediate, same four bfloat16 rounding
96|  points and positional `y[r,j]`.
97|
98|## Which inefficiency it removes, and how
99|
100|- `ineff-baseline-experts-2` (chained 1-row latency): attempt-5's
101|  miss analysis left the still-sequential down chain as the
102|  largest named remainder at 1 row — 12 strided steps × 2 waves
103|  behind the silu barrier, plus the `tg_x` load, silu, barriers
104|  and chained fixed cost. Attempts 1–3 showed threadgroup count
105|  past 4 is not the lever and attempt-4/5 showed overlapping the
106|  per-block serial K chain is. The down product was the last
107|  product still running its blocks in fully sequential waves with
108|  only one block's loads in flight per simdgroup; merging two
109|  blocks per simdgroup puts both blocks' loads (8 weight words +
110|  2 scales/biases per step) in flight in every step, so each
111|  block's load latency has the other block's loads/compute to
112|  hide behind, without touching any block's `simd_sum` order.
113|  The shared-`q` fix is what lets this merged loop launch at all:
114|  attempt-6 proved the three-array form exceeds the pipeline
115|  threadgroup budget at 512 threads.
116|- `ineff-baseline-experts-1` (prefill G2 gate): already removed by
117|  attempt-5's branch; kept by reusing its scalar `qmm_accum`
118|  verbatim — the interleave does not touch prefill arithmetic.
119|- `ineff-baseline-experts-3` (per-pair re-reads): deliberately
120|  kept, as in attempts 1–6 — weight bytes per pair stay 552,960 B;
121|  the interleave changes load scheduling, not bytes.
122|
123|## Limits (by hand; the grader does not check the 32 KB cap)
124|
125|512 threads/group ≤ 1,024 (`spec.json` identical to attempt-5/6).
126|Threadgroup memory unchanged: `tg_x[768] + tg_gate[384] +
127|tg_up[384] + tg_h[384]` bfloat16 = **3,840 B** of 32,768 B,
128|rows-independent. Distinct thread arrays are two 32-float
129|accumulators (`p`, shared `q`) — attempt-5's count, one fewer than
130|attempt-6's three. Grid scales as `rows*4` groups, so the kernel
131|is valid at every `rows ≥ 1`, on both sides of 60. Decode coverage:
132|12 simdgroups × 2 blocks × 32 lanes = 768 outputs per pair, each
133|written exactly once, as before.
134|
135|## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (chained, grader timing)
136|
137|Attempt-5 (other run): 92.1 / 162.0 / 534.8 µs/layer vs compiled
138|75.9 / 234.6 / 798.2 and reference 95.7 / 232.4 / 802.3. Attempt-6
139|predicted 85 / 156 / 540 but never launched, so that prediction is
140|untested, not missed. Baseline `none`, so no
141|`wins_vs_baseline` / `beats_baseline`. Weight bytes per layer
142|(552,960 B/pair): 2.21 / 17.69 / 70.78 MB at 4 / 32 / 128 pairs;
143|bandwidth floors at 200 GB/s: 11.1 / 88.5 / 353.9 µs.
144|Attempt-5 effective: 24.0 / 109.2 / 132.3 GB/s.
145|
146|Down arithmetic: `K = 384` → 12 strided steps per lane per block.
147|Attempt-5 pays 2 waves × 12 steps sequentially after the silu
148|barrier; this attempt pays 12 merged steps. A merged step issues
149|twice the loads (8 weight words, 2 scales) for twice the
150|accumulate work, so it costs more than a single-block step but
151|less than two — the gate/up precedent (attempt-4) hid ≈ 20% of
152|the merged chain's exposed latency at 1 row.
153|
154|- **1 row: 85.** Latency-bound (floor 11.1 µs). The down phase
155|  sits alone behind the silu barrier; at attempt-5's 92.1 µs the
156|  product chains (gate/up merged 24 steps + down 2×12 steps)
157|  dominate, so the down waves are roughly a third of the layer
158|  (≈ 30 µs). Collapsing 24 sequential steps into 12 merged ones
159|  at ≈ 1.3× the per-step cost (8 loads share the `tg_h[k]` read
160|  and the loop control) cuts the down phase to ≈ 23 µs, saving
161|  ≈ 7 µs → 92.1 − 7 ≈ **85 µs**. Still above compiled 75.9 — the
162|  `tg_x` load, silu, barriers and chained launch/link cost
163|  remain untouched — but it should roughly halve the 16.2 µs gap.
164|  The shared `q` itself is arithmetic-neutral; its only timing
165|  effect is restoring a legal 512-thread pipeline.
166|- **8 rows: 156.** 32 groups per call partly hide one group's
167|  down tail behind other groups' K loops (attempt-5 already at
168|  109.2 GB/s), so only part of the 1-row saving survives:
169|  162.0 − 6 ≈ **156 µs**, keeping the win over compiled 234.6.
170|- **32 rows: 540.** Streaming-bound (attempt-5: 132.3 GB/s).
171|  Group parallelism already hides load latency, so the merged
172|  loop buys nothing; the peak live accumulator count is the same
173|  64 floats gate/up already held in attempt-5, so no new spill
174|  tax is expected beyond attempt-6's identical merged step:
175|  534.8 + 5 ≈ **540 µs**, keeping the win over compiled 798.2.
176|
177|G1 prediction: pass — the launch is attempt-5's (512 threads,
178|3,840 B threadgroup memory) and the only change from attempt-5's
179|register footprint is that down now also holds a second live
180|accumulator, which gate/up already held in the same kernel that
181|launched at 512; the distinct-array count is attempt-5's two,
182|not attempt-6's three.
183|G2 prediction: pass at all six sizes with `differ == 0` — each
184|down block's dequant terms, add order and `simd_sum` are
185|attempt-5's by construction (separate logical accumulators,
186|shared storage re-zeroed per call), gate/up and prefill are
187|byte-identical to attempt-5's, and the parallel store writes the
188|same `(bfloat)p[j]` values, just one merged loop earlier.
189|
190|## Verdict
191|
192|G1 pass; **G2 pass at all six sizes, differ 0 / max_ulp 0.0
193|everywhere** (decode 1/8/32 and prefill 127/1,016/2,048 — no first
194|difference, `experts` reports the first differing element only on
195|failure and there is none) — the shared-storage rename preserves
196|attempt-5/6 bits by construction and the grader confirms it: the
197|merged down loop's per-block order and the parallel stores are
198|bit-exact, and the `rows >= 60` scalar `qmm_accum` branch is
199|untouched. The 512-thread launch now compiles: sharing one
200|kernel-scope `q[32]` between gate/up's second accumulator and
201|down's second block restores the pipeline's threadgroup budget
202|that attempt-6's three distinct arrays exceeded (512 > 448).
203|Chained timing µs/layer (this run; candidate vs reference vs
204|compiled): **1 row 93.8 / 78.9 / 74.8 (loses to compiled by
205|19.0, loses to reference by 14.9)**; 8 rows 160.1 / 235.8 /
206|236.5 (wins); 32 rows 510.1 / 797.0 / 792.7 (wins).
207|`beats_compiled` false — only the 1-row size misses, as in
208|attempt-5. Baseline `none` — no `wins_vs_baseline` /
209|`beats_baseline`.
210|
211|Against attempt-5 (different run; compiled shifted 75.9 → 74.8
212|at 1 row and 798.2 → 792.7 at 32 rows between runs, so treat
213|cross-run deltas as indicative): 93.8 vs 92.1 at 1 row
214|(**+1.8%**), 160.1 vs 162.0 at 8 rows (**−1.2%**), 510.1 vs
215|534.8 at 32 rows (**−4.6%**). Effective bandwidth on pair
216|bytes: 23.6 / 110.5 / 138.8 GB/s (attempt-5: 24.0 / 109.2 /
217|132.3). The down interleave therefore helps where group
218|parallelism already hides load latency (32 rows, +4.9% GB/s,
219|new best 32-row time in this hypothesis) and is neutral at
220|8 rows, but it does not move the latency-bound 1-row size.
221|
222|## Miss analysis (prediction 85 / 156 / 540, measured 93.8 / 160.1 / 510.1)
223|
224|Misses are +10.4% / +2.6% / −5.5% — all inside the 20% bar, so
225|no formal miss, but the size pattern was inverted versus the
226|prediction (saving predicted largest at 1 row, actually largest
227|at 32 rows) and that needs explaining:
228|
229|1. **The compilation fix worked exactly as predicted, the
230|   latency saving did not.** G1 passes at 512 threads with the
231|   same 3,840 B of threadgroup memory, confirming attempt-6's
232|   failure was the third distinct accumulator array, not
233|   threadgroup memory or the merged loop itself: two distinct
234|   arrays (`p`, shared `q`) fit, three do not. That part of the
235|   prediction (pure rename, identical bits) is confirmed by
236|   G2's differ 0 at all six sizes.
237|2. **At 1 row the down waves were not a third of the layer's
238|   latency in the way the arithmetic assumed.** The prediction
239|   priced the down phase at ≈ 30 µs and the merged step at
240|   1.3× a single-block step. Measured 93.8 ≈ attempt-5's 92.1
241|   says the merged step costs closer to 2× at this size: with
242|   only 4 threadgroups (one per pair) on 16 cores, the down
243|   phase's latency was already hidden *across* simdgroups —
244|   attempt-5's wave 0 runs 16 blocks concurrently per group,
245|   attempt-7 runs 12 simdgroups each serially merging two
246|   blocks, so concurrent in-flight loads per group fall
247|   (48 vs 64 simdgroup-block chains per call at 1 row) while
248|   each chain's step doubles its loads. The gate/up precedent
249|   hid ≈ 20% because gate and up *share* the `tg_x[k]` read and
250|   both blocks' loads were previously fully sequential phases;
251|   down's two blocks share only `tg_h[k]` and already overlapped
252|   across the 16-simdgroup wave. The remaining ≈ 19 µs gap to
253|   compiled (93.8 vs 74.8) is therefore still the `tg_x` load,
254|   silu, the two barriers and the chained launch/link cost —
255|   none of which this change touches.
256|3. **At 32 rows the merged loop pays for a different reason.**
257|   One wave instead of two removes a wave-quantization tail
258|   (wave 1 ran 8 of 16 simdgroups) on every pair and halves the
259|   down loop's barrier-free step count, which at 128 groups
260|   shows up as throughput: 138.8 vs 132.3 GB/s. The predicted
261|   +5 µs register tax did not appear (measured −24.7 µs vs
262|   attempt-5 cross-run) — consistent with the shared `q`: peak
263|   live accumulators never exceed gate/up's 64 floats, so there
264|   is no new spill, and claim 2's cross-simdgroup overlap loss
265|   is hidden by group parallelism at this size.
266|
267|Lesson for `ineff-baseline-experts-2`: a merged pair helps only
268|where the two blocks were previously *phases* (gate then up,
269|fully sequential, shared activation read); where the blocks
270|already ran as concurrent simdgroups in one wave (down's 24
271|blocks), merging trades cross-simdgroup parallelism for
272|in-step parallelism and is latency-neutral at 4 groups — the
273|1-row remainder is fixed cost and the serial gate/up chain,
274|not the down wave count. Register headroom at 512 threads is
275|exactly two 32-float accumulators; a third distinct array,
276|however short-lived, fails G1.
277|
278|## Next change
279|
280|Leave the down interleave in (it is the best 32-row time and
281|G2-exact) and attack the actual 1-row remainder named above:
282|the `tg_x` load + silu + barrier chain and the chained fixed
283|cost. Concretely, overlap the down product's first K steps with
284|the silu tail (down blocks whose `tg_h` slice is already
285|written) or narrow the silu barrier to a simdgroup-local one —
286|but any such change must keep the full-bfloat16 silu bits and
287|every accumulation order, and must not add a third accumulator
288|array (this attempt's G1 lesson).

37:- **routing attempt-4 passed G3 as it stood, on decode steps.** It is faster than both the unchanged model and the compiled reference at 1, 8 and 32 requests, in both engines. In vLLM it saves 0.47, 0.43 and 0.54 ms per step (8.7%, 3.0% and 1.8%). It is the project's first Muse kernel that passed every rule of its time. Over whole requests its gain is smaller, since it processes prompts 7–10% slower: throughput rises 10.2% with 1 request and 1.8% with 8, is flat with 32 and falls 3.5% with 32 requests of 1,024-token prompts ([section 5](#5-whole-requests-prompts-and-throughput)). Under the rule set after this measurement, that an improvement must hold in both phases ([ADR 0011](../adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)), it fails, so it is no baseline for round 3 ([For round 3](#for-round-3-baselines-and-starting-points)).
59:`check_sizes.py` applies the grader's bit-exact checks to every layer's slot inputs in the first N tokens of a one-request prefill (`sizes-check.json`). The 25 values of N are:
158:**The rule,** from round 3 ([ADR 0011](../adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)): a slot's baseline is its best attempt so far that passes the current G2, has `beats_compiled` true in the grader, and passes G3. Both of those now judge two phases, decode and prefill: faster in one, slower in neither, and in G3 no whole request slower, against the unchanged model and the compiled reference. 10|

The compiled references installed the same way stay within ±0.29 ms of additive, so composing three replacements is not by itself the cost. 1|# Round 1 of the Muse agent, measured
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|In round 1 (2026-11-03), the Muse agent (Muse Spark, `muse-spark-1.3-contributor`) explored the decode step as a swarm, then wrote fused Metal kernels for three slots of the mixture-of-experts block. Its summary, [muse-spark/summary.md](../../muse-spark/summary.md), names one final attempt per slot. Each one passed the grader, and the summary predicted, from the per-slot timing, that together they would shorten the decode step by 0.54, 1.81 and 5.72 ms at 1, 8 and 32 requests.
6|
7|This is Claude's independent measurement of those three attempts, done on main after merging round 1 (`a4995e4`), on 2026-11-04:
8|- **re-grading** them with the grader;
9|- **checking them end to end** in the model, in plain MLX and in vLLM;
10|- **timing the decode step (G3)** with each slot alone and with all three together.
11|
12|It is the measurement that round 2's skill reads first: the last section names what round 2 starts from in each slot.
13|
14|**Where everything is.** The raw data is in [results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-1/](../../results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-1/). The scripts are:
15|- `bench/grader/check_candidate.py`, the grader;
16|- `bench/grader/time_candidates.py`, the end-to-end check and G3;
17|- `bench/micro/chain_timing.py`, the chained-timing experiment.
18|
19|**The machine.** The M1 Pro measured the baseline ([method](../benchmark/method.md)). Docker was quit for these runs, with surucuonur's permission. Another job of surucuonur's was running, and 21.3 to 22.7 GB of the 22.5 to 23.5 GB of swap were in use (`machine-*.txt`). vLLM ran with `VLLM_METAL_KV_COMMIT_PROBE=0`, as in earlier runs.
20|
21|## Summary
22|
23|- **All three attempts pass the grader as round 1 ran it.** On main, each one compiles, matches the reference within G2's tolerances at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and beats the compiled reference in the per-slot timing.
24|- **In the model, all three together make the decode step slower with 1 and 8 requests.** In vLLM:
25|  - +0.98 ms (+18%) with 1 request;
26|  - +0.16 ms (+1%) with 8;
27|  - −1.76 ms (−6%) with 32.
28|
29|  Round 1 predicted −0.54, −1.81 and −5.72 ms.
30|- **The experts kernel alone slows the step by 1.2 ms (22%) with 1 request,** although the grader timed it 36% faster than the reference.
31|  - The grader ran the 20 layers' calls with nothing between them, so the GPU overlapped them.
32|  - In the model each layer waits for the one before. Chained like that, the kernel takes 133 µs per layer against the reference's 80.
33|- **Each attempt changes the model's tokens,** breaking the brief's end-to-end rule. With 32 requests in vLLM, each one alone changes 7 to 12 of the 32 sequences from the first generated token.
34|  - **experts:** the prefill runs the same slot at 127 to 2,048 rows. There, MLX's own experts kernel changes, and the attempt differs from the reference in 62% of its outputs. The grader tested decode sizes only.
35|  - **routing and combine:** their small rounding differences, within G2's tolerances, are enough to flip greedy tokens.
36|- **The grader changes for round 2** ([ADR 0010](../adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md)). G2 is now bit-exact and also covers the prefill's sizes, and the timing chains the layers. None of round 1's attempts passes the new G2.
37|- **Round 2 has no baseline in any slot.** Its bar is the compiled reference. Round 1's three final attempts are its starting points.
38|- **Round 1 ran the grader 29 times on the experts slot** for the 4 attempts its summary counts, 18 of those on attempt-1.
39|
40|## 1. The grader, as round 1 ran it
41|
42|Re-run on main with the grader of `a4995e4` (`grade-<slot>.json`). µs per layer: reference / compiled reference / attempt.
43|
44|| Slot, attempt | 1 row | 8 rows | 32 rows | G1, G2 |
45||---|---|---|---|---|
46|| experts, attempt-4 | 143.8 / 139.5 / **92.1** | 222.5 / 221.4 / **165.4** | 770.1 / 762.4 / **529.9** | pass, pass (0 units in the last place) |
47|| routing, attempt-1 | 39.9 / 31.5 / **25.3** | 83.5 / 42.7 / **24.3** | 101.2 / 87.6 / **68.9** | pass, pass (weights within 2.6×10⁻⁶) |
48|| combine, attempt-1 | 23.1 / 23.8 / **18.6** | 22.5 / 26.1 / **17.0** | 39.5 / 32.0 / **18.9** | pass, pass (up to 2 units) |

51|
52|## 2. End to end: the tokens
53|
54|`time_candidates.py` installs each attempt in every layer's `MoE.__call__`, and generates 24 greedy tokens after 128-token prompts. It does this for each slot alone, for all three together, and for each slot's compiled reference. The brief's G2 asks for the same tokens as the unchanged model. Sequences that differ, and the first generated token where one does (`muse-plain.jsonl`, `muse-vllm.jsonl`, records of kind `check`):
55|
56|| Variant | Plain MLX, 1 request | Plain MLX, 32 | vLLM, 1 | vLLM, 32 |
57||---|---|---|---|---|
58|| experts attempt-4 | 1, from token 2 | 19, from token 0 | 0 | 12, from token 0 |
59|| routing attempt-1 | 1, from token 2 | 7, from token 1 | 0 | 9, from token 0 |
60|| combine attempt-1 | 1, from token 2 | 5, from token 2 | 0 | 7, from token 0 |
61|| all three | 0 | 19, from token 0 | 0 | 13, from token 0 |
62|| every compiled reference | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
63|
64|The compiled references give the same tokens in every case, so the unchanged model is deterministic, and every difference comes from the attempts.
65|
66|**Why the tokens change.** Greedy decoding picks the most likely next token. On these random-token prompts, the top two candidates are often very close, so any change to the numbers can flip the choice, and every later token follows from it. That gives two causes:
67|
68|- **The prefill (measured).** The model's prefill runs `MoE.__call__` on the prompt in chunks. With 128-token prompts and 2,048-token chunks, that is 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows at 1, 8 and 32 requests.
69|  - **From the code:** from 60 rows on, MLX switches its experts kernel from `gather_qvm` to `gather_qmm_rhs`, which rounds differently. Round 1's own analysis found this threshold (`muse-spark/exploration/territory-switch-layers.md`, section G).
70|  - **The attempt:** experts attempt-4 copies `gather_qvm`'s arithmetic exactly, which is why it is bit-exact at decode sizes. With the prefill's inputs, it differs from the reference in 62% of its outputs, by up to 110 units in the last place (`grade-exact-experts.json`).
71|  - **The grader:** it never tested more than 32 rows.
72|- **Small rounding differences (measured).** routing attempt-1 picks the same experts in the same order, but every row's weights differ from the reference's, by up to 2.6×10⁻⁶ at decode sizes and 8.7×10⁻⁶ in the prefill. combine attempt-1 differs in 2 to 130 elements per size. Both are inside G2's old tolerances, and both still change 5 to 9 of 32 sequences.
73|

75|
