5|# Muse Spark works in Muse Code, Meta's own coding agent, with helper agents and no attempt limit
6|
7|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*
8|
9|*[ADR 0007](0007-muse-spark-swarm.md) replaces this record's round design on 2026-11-03, before round 1: a swarm of explorers and builders instead of short-lived helpers. That covers the helpers, the drafts, `diagnosis.md`, `strategy.md` and grading by the lead alone. Muse Code, the launcher, the isolation and the lack of an attempt limit stand.*
10|
11|**The change.** From 2026-11-02, Muse Spark does its kernel work in **Muse Code** ([Meta's docs](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code)), not in a Claude Code session pointed at Meta. This replaces [ADR 0004](0004-muse-spark-as-claude-code-agent.md) and [ADR 0005](0005-muse-spark-launcher-only-contributor-tier.md) wherever they describe the harness.
12|- surucuonur starts it with [tools/muse-agent/start.sh](../../tools/muse-agent/start.sh), still the only way in.
13|- Every round follows the skill [.agents/skills/muse-round/SKILL.md](../../.agents/skills/muse-round/SKILL.md). Claude wrote the skill, and it is committed in the repository so anyone can read it. In each round:
14|  1. Muse's helper agents investigate the run evidence and the code, each with the surrounding system in view.
15|  2. Muse writes a diagnosis and a strategy.
16|  3. Helpers draft and review kernels, and the lead grades and commits them.
17|
18|## Why
19|
20|- **Only Meta's tools on the Muse side.** The hackathon scores "Use of Meta AI tooling", and its FAQ names Muse Code.
21|- **Claude Code's own prompt stops going to Meta.** With Claude Code as the harness, Anthropic's system prompt and tool definitions went to Meta with every request. On the contributor tier, Meta may train on them, which sits uncomfortably with Anthropic's terms (ADR 0004).
22|- **Helper agents.** surucuonur wants the investigation and the kernel work spread over several agents. Muse Code has native subagents: up to 8 at once by default, the lead included. Its scripted workflows are missing from the Apple Silicon build.
23|
24|## What changes in the brief
25|
26|The [brief](../muse-agent-brief.md) stays fixed as committed, and so do its task, slots, tools, files, grader and the pass criteria G1 and G2. Three things change:
27|
28|1. **The harness.** The brief's "You are a Claude Code session" and "the co-author trailer your settings add" now read: a Muse Code session that writes the trailer itself. Muse Code has no setting that adds it, so the skill gives the exact commit command, and `commit-msg` refuses a `muse-agent` commit without it.
29|2. **No attempt limit and no stop rule.** In surucuonur's words: "if we limit the model, it should be limitless inside the muse code, it should stop with muse codes stopping conditions."
30|   - Muse works until it judges a slot done, or until Muse Code stops. No step cap is set, and surucuonur can interrupt at any time.
31|   - **What keeps it honest:** every graded attempt is committed, in order. The summary gives the number of graded attempts per slot, so readers see how many tries the best result came from.
32|3. **Drafts and a diagnosis.** Helpers write candidate kernels in `muse-spark/drafts/`. These are never graded on their own and are committed with the attempt they fed. `muse-spark/diagnosis.md` names the root cause per slot before any kernel is written.
33|
34|## How the work stays apart
35|
36|- **Starting over.** The `muse-agent` branch from the Claude Code harness was deleted on surucuonur's decision: one strategy commit and one ungraded attempt, "didnt start properly and didnt do much work". The new `muse-agent` starts from the tag `muse-code-era`, so every Muse result comes from Muse Code.
37|- **Place.**
38|  - Its own worktree, `../Hackathon-muse`, on `muse-agent`; writes only in `muse-spark/`, enforced by `pre-commit`.
39|  - The launcher trusts the worktree for each run, which loads the project skill and allows helpers.
40|  - It gives `muse` a home folder of its own, `~/.muse-spark`, which holds its settings and session logs. Muse Code looks for personal skills and rules under the home folder (`~/.agents/skills`, `~/.claude/skills`, `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`) and loads them by default; in its own home it finds none, so the model sees only Muse Code's bundled skills and the project's skill.
41|- **Key.** `MODEL_API_KEY` from `legal-agent-workshop/agent/.env` goes only to the `muse` process, as `META_API_KEY`, and is never stored.
42|- **Seeing Claude's newest work.** `muse-agent` can't take merges. After a round, its branch is merged into main with `--no-ff` and Claude commits its results as `claude/findings/muse-round-<N>.md`. The next launch then fast-forwards `muse-agent` to main, which creates no commit and rewrites nothing, so the next round reads those results.
43|- **One GPU job at a time.** The grader takes an exclusive lock ([bench/grader/gpu_lock.py](../../bench/grader/gpu_lock.py)), so a second run, from any agent or from Claude, stops with a message instead of distorting the timings. Only the lead grades.
44|- **Evidence.** Muse Code logs every model call, tool run and edit for the lead, each helper and its own reminder agents, one log per agent, and `muse export` writes a log as JSON. [tools/export_transcript.py](../../tools/export_transcript.py) joins a session's logs into one transcript in `muse-spark/transcripts/`.
45|  - **What it keeps:** messages, tool calls and results, approvals, and the model of each call.
46|  - **What it drops:** Muse Code's own instructions.
47|  - It refuses a session that contains a key.
48|  - The audit checks that a Meta model (`muse-*`) made every model call.
49|- **Unchanged:** the authorship, the trailers, the hooks, the audit, and Claude's independent re-grading and G3 after each merge.
50|
51|## Consequences
52|
53|- **The model:** `muse-spark-1.3-contributor`, as in ADR 0005, for round 1; from round 2, `muse-wonder-1.0` on the same API key ([ADR 0008](0008-muse-wonder.md)). Meta may train on everything sent: the brief, the skill, the findings and every file Muse reads, all written by Claude or by us. Claude Code's own prompt is no longer among them. surucuonur accepted this for the lower price.
54|- **No sandbox.** Muse Code's sandbox keeps `.git` read-only, and a worktree commits into the main checkout's `.git`, so the launcher passes `--disable-sandbox`. Tool approvals stay on.
55|  - **Remaining risk:** an approved shell command can reach what the account can, and the key is in the session's environment. Every commit and exported transcript is scanned for it.
56|- **No fallback.** If Muse Code can't run the round, the fix is in the Muse Code setup. surucuonur ruled out returning to the Claude Code harness.
57|- **Superset's notification hooks,** set in surucuonur's own Muse Code settings, don't run in Muse Spark's sessions, which use their own home and settings.
58|- **The first smoke test leaked personal context.** It ran with Muse Code's settings for leaving personal skills and rules out, which turned out not to work. surucuonur's global instructions and the names and descriptions of 43 personal skills went to Meta. See [PROVENANCE.md](../../PROVENANCE.md).
59|
60|## Considered options
61|
62|- **Keep the Claude Code harness (ADR 0004/0005).** It already worked, but Anthropic's prompt goes to Meta, and the Muse side isn't Meta's tooling.
63|- **Keep the old branch as an archive,** renamed and pushed. Rejected: its work was too slight to keep beside a fresh start.
64|- **Keep the brief's 5 attempts per slot and its stop rule.** Rejected by surucuonur; the full commit history and the attempt counts replace the limit as the safeguard.
65|- **Let helpers grade too.** The GPU times one run at a time, so parallel grading adds coordination and no speed.
66|- **Muse Code's own settings for personal skills and rules,** `context.foreign_personal_skills` and `context.foreign_personal_rules`. Briefly adopted, then replaced after the first smoke test on 2026-11-03.
67|  - Muse Code 1.4.14 accepts them with `-c`, but personal skills and rules still load.
68|  - They name only other agents' folders. `~/.agents/skills` counts as Muse Code's own and would load anyway.
69|  - The flag `--no-foreign-personal-context` does drop `~/.claude`, but only for headless runs, and it also leaves `~/.agents/skills`.

5|# Muse Spark's round is a swarm: explorers share one analysis, then competing builders grade their own kernels
6|
7|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*
8|
9|*From round 2, each round writes its shared documents in its own folder, finished rounds are frozen, and attempts must beat the best attempt so far ([ADR 0009](0009-rounds-build-on-each-other.md)); the model becomes Muse Wonder ([ADR 0008](0008-muse-wonder.md)). The swarm itself is unchanged.*
10|
11|**The change.** From 2026-11-03, before round 1, the round skill ([.agents/skills/muse-round/](../../.agents/skills/muse-round/SKILL.md)) runs a **swarm**. This replaces the lead with short-lived helpers that [ADR 0006](0006-muse-spark-in-muse-code.md) described. The round has two phases, in surucuonur's words:
12|
13|- **Exploration.** "Point individual agents at individual codebases (modules within codebases, or even individual files if its too important) and measurement documentations."
14|  - Together they write one analysis that all of them can read and change, "so that they can change direction for more focusing".
15|  - Its final version holds "the context, analysis, relations, possible inefficiency and everything … for future improvements".
16|- **Implementation.** From the analysis, build "the best solution that can be implemented in here, by using multiple agents to build it".
17|  - It must be "aware of the full system" and must not "affect the previous or after steps".
18|  - "The best version of the solution should be ready to test and go."
19|
20|surucuonur also asked that both phases be "trackable by the documents … so that I can track their findings".
21|
22|## How the swarm works
23|
24|- **One Muse Code session.**
25|  - The lead starts the helpers, keeps the phase documents current, settles clashes, and is the only agent that commits.
26|  - It neither explores nor grades.
27|  - The launcher raises Muse Code's limit from 8 agents at once to 12.
28|- **Exploration.**
29|  - One explorer per **territory**: a module, a single important file, or a measurement document.
30|  - There are 8 to start: the model, the expert path, MLX's quantized kernels, MLX's other slot kernels, vllm-metal's decode path, the grader's slot interface, Claude's findings, and the other runs.
31|  - The lead splits, merges or adds territories as costs show up.
32|  - A verifier marks each inefficiency confirmed or refuted against its sources.
33|  - Implementation starts once every territory is done and every inefficiency is settled.
34|- **Implementation.**
35|  - Confirmed inefficiencies are taken in order of predicted saving, at most two at a time and in different slots.
36|  - Per inefficiency, a boundary agent first writes what the solution must keep identical: the slot's inputs and outputs, dtypes, rounding points, and the steps before and after.
37|  - Then 2 or 3 builders each take a different direction, and each writes and grades its own attempt.
38|  - The best attempt is hardened one change at a time until it passes G1, G2 and the boundary check, and beats the compiled reference at 1, 8 and 32 rows.
39|  - No limit, as in ADR 0006: the lead ends the round when it judges further work won't pay, and says why.
40|- **Adapting.** Before every new task and after every post, an agent reads its phase's tracker and the newest log lines. It changes direction when:
41|  - another entry already covers its item;
42|  - its premise was refuted;
43|  - an unowned item predicts a larger saving.
44|  
45|  Savings are compared in µs per decode step at 1, 8 and 32 rows.
46|
47|## The shared documents
48|
49|`muse-spark/exploration/` and `muse-spark/implementation/` each hold:
50|- **`README.md`.** The phase's document, opening with a tracker table. Exploration's is the analysis; implementation's is the report, ending with the solution that is ready to test. Only the lead writes it, so concurrent edits never clobber it.
51|- **Entries,** one file per territory, inefficiency or hypothesis. Each has a status block its owner keeps current, and other agents append notes under `## From other agents` rather than rewriting.
52|- **`log.md`.** One line per event from every agent, appended through the shell: 2,000 concurrent appends from two writers, tested, came out whole.
53|
54|The files are live in the worktree while the round runs (`tail -f …/log.md`), and the lead commits them at every checkpoint.
55|
56|## Versions
57|
58|surucuonur asked for version numbers that git commits control. Each version is raised by a single writer, so no number is taken twice:
59|- **Phase versions:**
60|  - each README opens with its version, vN, and the skill version the round runs;
61|  - the lead raises it at every checkpoint, and each version is exactly one commit, whose subject names it (`Muse Spark: exploration v5: …`);
62|  - the README ends with a changelog naming the entries each version changed.
63|- **Entry versions:**
64|  - each entry's status block has a version, which its owner raises with every change to its own text;
65|  - the verifier raises it with its verdict, and the lead raises it for hypothesis entries;
66|  - notes from other agents leave it alone.
67|- **Skill versions:**
68|  - the skill folder carries one number, raised by Claude with every change ([CHANGELOG.md](../../.agents/skills/muse-round/CHANGELOG.md)), and each round records the version it ran;
69|  - this design is version 2, and versioning arrived in version 3.
70|- **No tags for versions.** Tags stay for the era markers (`agent-era`, `muse-code-era`), and Muse Spark creates none.
71|
72|## What changes in the brief, beyond ADR 0006
73|
74|- **`strategy.md` and its targets JSON give way to hypothesis entries.** No code reads the JSON.
75|- **`diagnosis.md` gives way to the exploration folder.**
76|- **No drafts.** Every solution a builder finishes is graded and committed as an attempt, so the attempt count includes all of them.
77|- **Builders grade.** `bench/grader/gpu_lock.py` now waits for its turn instead of exiting when the GPU is busy. Runs queue and never overlap, so the timings stay clean. The grader is still the only GPU job, and helpers load no model.
78|
79|The task, the slots, the grader, G1 and G2 stay.
80|
81|## Consequences
82|
83|- **More model calls:** about 10 agents in exploration, and up to 9 in implementation. Meta's terms for the contributor tier are unchanged (ADR 0006).
84|- **A GPU queue:** a builder may wait for others' grading. One run takes under 3 minutes.
85|- **Approvals:** all agents' shell commands surface in surucuonur's one terminal.
86|- **Lost edits:** two agents appending to one entry at the same moment can still lose a note. The lead re-reads at each checkpoint.
87|- **Only the lead commits,** because simultaneous commits from one checkout collide on git's index lock.
88|
89|## Considered options
90|
91|- **Perspectives by kind of cost** (bytes, launches, routing, occupancy, correctness, a skeptic). Proposed first; surucuonur chose territories of the code and measurements instead.
92|- **Separate Muse Code sessions with no lead.** True peers, but one terminal of approvals per session, split transcripts, and no one to settle clashes.
93|- **Only the lead grades.** No grader change, but the lead becomes the bottleneck.
94|- **One shared file, or one `analysis.md` written at the end.** One file lets simultaneous edits drop each other's changes, and an end-only document can't be followed live.

5|# From round 2, the Muse agent is Muse Wonder, on the Meta Model API
6|
7|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*
8|
9|*[ADR 0012](0012-muse-spark-contributor-unattended.md) replaces this record's model choice on 2026-11-04, after round 2: from round 3 the launcher runs Muse Spark's contributor model again, with tool approvals off. Round 2 ran Muse Wonder as recorded here.*
10|
11|**The change.** From round 2 (decided 2026-11-03), the launcher runs **Muse Wonder** (`muse-wonder-1.0`) instead of Muse Spark (`muse-spark-1.3-contributor`, round 1). surucuonur asked for Meta's best model, wanting "to see improved results after this step". Meta calls Muse Wonder "Meta's most capable model" ([Meta's model docs](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/models)).
12|
13|surucuonur first chose Muse Wonder Full, "the higher-capability variant", and the launcher was set up for it. Full "is available only in Muse Code with a subscription", so it needs a Muse Code sign-in. surucuonur then chose to run without a sign-in: "without login switch to Muse Wonder in the api". No session ran with Full.
14|
15|## How it runs
16|
17|- **Sign-in.** The same pay-as-you-go API key as round 1 (`MUSE_AUTH=key`, the launcher's default), read from `legal-agent-workshop/agent/.env` and given only to `muse`.
18|- **The model id** is `muse-wonder-1.0` (`MUSE_MODEL`), from [Meta's price list](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/pricing-rate-limits). A one-prompt smoke test confirms that the key may call it before round 2.
19|- **Reasoning effort `max`** (`MUSE_EFFORT`): Muse Wonder "supports reasoning effort levels from "minimal" to "max"". Round 1 ran at Muse Code's default, `high`.
20|- **No contributor mode.** It is a subscription setting, so the launcher passes `--contributor-mode` only with `MUSE_AUTH=account`. Meta's standard API terms apply to what is sent; everything the agents read is public in this repository, as in round 1.
21|- The model and effort are passed on the command line, so the session log records them.
22|- **Full stays possible:** `MUSE_AUTH=account`, `MUSE_MODEL=muse-wonder-full-1.0` and one `MUSE_AUTH=account tools/muse-agent/start.sh login`. That id is unconfirmed: Meta's pages give none for Full, and it comes from a third-party page.
23|
24|## Naming the author
25|
26|surucuonur chose to name the real model wherever the author is identified.
27|- **The co-author line** for round 2 is `Co-Authored-By: Muse Wonder (Meta Model API) <muse-wonder@meta-model-api.invalid>`, and commit subjects start with "Muse Wonder:". Round 1's commits keep "Muse Spark (Meta Model API)".
28|- **Where it comes from.** `tools/provenance.py` maps each model id prefix to its name and co-author line (`MUSE_AUTHORS`); the longest matching prefix wins, so `muse-wonder-full-` and `muse-wonder-` stay apart. The launcher puts both into the lead's first prompt, so the lead needn't know its own model id, and the transcript shows what it was told. No tool call in round 1 used an environment variable, so a variable set by the launcher couldn't be relied on.
29|- **The hooks and the audit** accept any Muse agent's co-author. The audit counts the commits of each.
30|- **"The Muse agent"** is the name for every model that works on `muse-agent` in a round. The paths `muse-spark/`, `muse-agent` and `~/.muse-spark` keep their names, so round 1's history and every path in its documents stay valid.
31|
32|## Consequences
33|
34|- **Price.** Billed per token: $4.00 per million input tokens, $0.20 cached and $20.00 output ([Meta's prices](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/pricing-rate-limits)), against $0.002, $0.10 and $0.20 for round 1's contributor model.
35|  - Round 1's tokens (86.8M input, 83.5M of them cached, and 1.04M output) cost about $0.70. The same tokens at Muse Wonder's prices cost about $50.
36|  - At `max` effort the output, the dearest part, is likely to grow; the round has no attempt limit, so the cost has no fixed ceiling. The session log counts the tokens.
37|- **Rate limits:** 3,000 requests and 4M tokens per minute per team, enough for 12 agents.
38|- **Round 2 changes several things at once:** the model, the effort, the skill (version 5, [ADR 0009](0009-rounds-build-on-each-other.md)) and the grader's rules ([ADR 0010](0010-exact-at-every-size.md)). A difference between the rounds can't be put down to the model alone, and the write-up says so.
39|- **Muse Wonder is in preview,** in Meta's words.
40|
41|## Considered options
42|
43|- **Muse Wonder Full through a Muse Code subscription.** The higher-capability variant at a flat monthly price, but it needs a sign-in and a Power Usage or Maximum Usage plan, its id is unconfirmed, and its allowance could run out mid-round. Chosen first, then dropped by surucuonur for the API.
44|- **Standard `muse-spark-1.3`.** Round 1's model family at about 12 times the contributor price. Rejected: not the most capable.
45|- **Keep "Muse Spark" as the co-author.** The smallest change, but round 2's commits would misname their model.
46|- **Rename the agent everywhere,** folder and branch included. It would rewrite paths that round 1's documents already use.

5|# Rounds build on each other: each in its own folder, finished rounds frozen, the best attempt so far is the bar
6|
7|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*
8|
9|**The change.** On 2026-11-03, before round 2, surucuonur asked that round 1's files stay the same, and that round 2 "can see the round 1 and its results" and "do different plan considering that". Under the round skill's version 3, round 2 would have done neither:
10|- it would have continued round 1's documents in place, with `## Round 2` sections in its entries, and its README versions, logs and summary carried on;
11|- it would have judged attempts only against the original MLX code and its compiled version, a bar round 1 already passed.
12|
13|Skill version 4 ([.agents/skills/muse-round/](../../.agents/skills/muse-round/SKILL.md)) changes both.
14|
15|## How it works
16|
17|- **A folder per round.** Round 1 stays at the top of `muse-spark/`. Round N writes in `muse-spark/round-<N>/`: `exploration/`, `implementation/`, `kernels/` and `summary.md`. Transcripts stay in `muse-spark/transcripts/`, one file per session.
18|- **Finished rounds are frozen.** Claude tags a round's last commit `muse-round-<N>` once its transcripts are committed. Round 1's tag is `muse-round-1`, on `60308aa`, and freezes its 71 files. From a tag on:
19|  - the pre-commit hook on `muse-agent` refuses any change to, or deletion of, a file the tag holds in `muse-spark/`. It also refuses a new file anywhere but the current round's folder and `muse-spark/transcripts/`;
20|  - the audit, `tools/provenance_check.py`, re-checks every commit after each tag, so a commit made around the hook is caught;
21|  - the transcript exporter skips sessions it has already exported, so running it again never rewrites a frozen transcript.
22|- **The starting point.** From round 2 on, the lead first writes a plan from:
23|  - the previous rounds' final documents;
24|  - the notes of each slot's best attempt;
25|  - Claude's report on the previous round, `claude/findings/muse-round-<N-1>.md`.
26|
27|  The plan covers, per slot, the best attempt so far (the **baseline**) and its G3 effect against its prediction. It also covers what is left to build, and which territories to explore again. The round stops if Claude's report is missing.
28|- **Targeted exploration.** Explorers map:
29|  - the baselines' kernels, now the code in the slots;
30|  - where Claude's G3 differed from the piece timing;
31|  - only those round-1 territories the plan reopens.
32|
33|  Earlier entries are cited, never rewritten.
34|- **The baseline is the bar.** Claude's report names each slot's baseline. A new attempt must beat it in the same grader run, with `bench/grader/check_candidate.py --baseline`.
35|  - **The test.** The two are timed in alternating repeats, so drift in the GPU's clocks reaches both alike. The candidate must be faster in at least 22 of the 30 paired repeats at each row count: a one-sided sign test at p < 0.01.
36|  - **Why a sign test.** In a test on 2026-11-03, round 1's combine attempt, timed separately against itself, differed by up to 5% between medians. In paired repeats it won only 15 to 19 of 30 against itself. Round 1's final experts attempt won 30 of 30 against its first. Comparing medians would have passed on noise.
37|- **A slot that nothing beats keeps its baseline** for G3.
38|
39|## Consequences
40|
41|- Round 1's files can't change, and every path in round 1's documents stays valid.
42|- Attempt numbers restart in each round's folder, and each round's summary counts attempts per round and over all rounds.
43|- The lead reads more at the start of a round, and the explorers repeat less.
44|- The grader's verdict gains `baseline`, `beats_baseline`, `wins_needed` and, per row count, `wins_vs_baseline`. Without `--baseline` it is unchanged.
45|- Claude's G3 for round 2 compares round 2's attempts with round 1's.
46|
47|## Considered options
48|
49|- **Carry on in round 1's folders** with `## Round N` sections, as version 3 did. Round 1's files would change, and only git history would keep their round-1 state.

5|# From round 2, a kernel must be bit-exact at every size it runs at, prefill included, and the piece timing chains the layers
6|
7|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*
8|
9|*[ADR 0011](0011-decode-and-prefill.md) changes two parts of this record on 2026-11-04, before round 3. An attempt may hand inputs above a row count it chooses to the compiled reference, instead of running its kernels in every call. The piece timing and G3 also time the prefill. Bit-exactness at every size and the chained timing stand.*
10|
11|**The change.** Claude's measurement of round 1 ([findings](../findings/muse-round-1.md)) found that round 1's final attempts, which passed the grader, broke the brief's end-to-end rule in the model, and that one of them slowed the decode step it was meant to speed up. The grader missed three things:
12|
13|1. **Sizes.** It tested a slot on a decode step's inputs only, at 1, 8 and 32 rows. The same `MoE.__call__` runs the prefill, at 127 to 2,048 rows with 128-token prompts. From 60 rows on, MLX's own experts kernel changes, from `gather_qvm` to `gather_qmm_rhs`, and so does its rounding. Round 1's experts kernel copied `gather_qvm` bit for bit, and differed in 62% of its outputs at each prefill size.
14|2. **Exactness.** G2 allowed small differences: 2 bfloat16 units in the last place, and 10⁻⁴ for routing weights. End to end, the brief asks for the same greedy tokens, and greedy decoding turns any difference into different tokens. Round 1's routing weights, within 10⁻⁵ of the reference, changed 7 to 9 of 32 sequences in 24 tokens.
15|3. **Latency.** The piece timing ran 20 layers' calls with no data between them, so the GPU could overlap them. At 1 row, round 1's experts kernel was 29% faster than the reference on overlapped calls and 66% slower on chained ones (`bench/micro/chain_timing.py`). In the model it slowed the decode step by 1.2 ms (22% in vLLM, 25% in plain MLX).
16|
17|On 2026-11-04 surucuonur chose, before round 2:
18|- **every call:** the kernels run wherever `MoE.__call__` runs, the prefill included;
19|- **bit-exact** outputs;
20|- **chained** piece timing.
21|
22|## How it works
23|
24|- **G2 at two kinds of size.** `bench/grader/check_candidate.py` checks every layer at:
25|  - the captured decode inputs, at 1, 8 and 32 rows;
26|  - the first prefill chunk at 1, 8 and 32 requests (127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows), recorded while it runs (`slots.capture_prefill`), with the prompts `time_candidates.py` uses.
27|- **Bit-exact.** An output passes only if it equals the reference's:
28|  - for routing, the 4 experts and their weights, in the same order, since combine sums the pairs in that order;
29|  - for combine and experts, every element.
30|
31|  The grader still reports the largest gap, in units in the last place, to help find the cause. The reference checked against itself shows no difference at any size.
32|- **Chained timing.** Each layer's call takes one input through `link`, a single fused kernel that adds 0 × one value of the previous call's output, so the call can't start before the previous one finishes. Every function timed (reference, compiled, candidate and baseline) gets the same link. The chained times match those of a real data chain within 10%.
33|  - **Why not `mx.depends`:** it orders only the graph. In a test on 2026-11-04, round 1's experts kernel took 46 µs per layer with it at 1 row, as fast as with no dependency, against 133 to 195 µs with a real data dependency in three runs.
34|- **The end-to-end check and G3 are unchanged.**
35|  - `bench/grader/time_candidates.py` now takes several `SLOT=FOLDER` attempts.
36|  - It times each slot alone, against its own compiled reference, and all of them together.
37|
38|## Consequences
39|
40|- **No round-1 attempt passes the new G2,** so round 2 has no baseline in any slot. Its bar is the compiled reference. Round 1's final attempts are its starting points, named in Claude's findings.
41|- **The experts slot needs a kernel exact at prefill sizes,** matching `gather_qmm_rhs`'s rounding from 60 rows on, or a single design whose rounding matches both of MLX's kernels.
42|- **A grader run takes longer.** It loads the model (760 MB) for every slot and runs three prefill chunks.
43|- **The piece timing now includes one small link kernel per layer** for every function timed. That brings the reference and the candidate closer in relative terms, but not in µs.
44|- **Not covered:** prefill speed. G3 times decode steps only, so a kernel slower at prefill sizes would go unnoticed, apart from the time to first token.
45|
46|## Considered options
47|
48|- **Decode calls only,** with MLX's code in the prefill. The kernels would need to be exact only at decode sizes, but they would no longer replace the whole MoE block. Not chosen: surucuonur asked for every call.
49|- **Keep the tolerances, and relax the token rule** to counting the sequences that differ. Simpler kernels, but the claim would become "the same model up to rounding", with a threshold to pick.
50|- **Keep independent timing,** and rely on G3 to catch latency. Round 2's builders would again rank attempts by a number that hid a 22% slowdown.
51|- **`mx.depends` for the chain.** No extra kernel, but it doesn't make the GPU wait.

5|# From round 3, an improvement must hold in both phases, decode and prefill, and an attempt may hand prefill-sized inputs to the compiled reference
6|
7|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*
8|
9|**The change.** Claude's comparison of every engine version over whole requests ([findings](../findings/muse-round-2.md), section 5) found that the grader and G3 timed only the decode step. They never timed the prefill, the phase in which a request's whole prompt runs through the model:
10|- **Experts attempt-7** looked like round 2's largest gain, a 19% shorter decode step at 32 requests. It processed prompts 6.6 to 14.5 times slower and cut throughput by 10% to 83%.
11|- **Routing attempt-4,** round 2's only baseline, processed prompts 7% to 10% slower. At 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts it cost 3.5% of throughput.
12|
13|The Muse agent never saw either effect: its piece timing ran decode sizes only, and G3 measured the decode step only.
14|
15|On 2026-11-04 surucuonur set the rule: "The improvement should be in the two phases of it: decode and prefill. Then, we can consider it as an improvement." surucuonur chose:
16|- **faster in one phase, slower in neither;**
17|- **the hand-off:** an attempt may leave prefill-sized inputs to the compiled reference. This replaces the part of [ADR 0010](0010-exact-at-every-size.md) that required the kernels to run in every call.
18|
19|## How it works
20|
21|- **The piece timing runs at the six G2 sizes** (`bench/grader/check_candidate.py`): decode at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and the first prefill chunk at 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. The layers are still chained.
22|- **The verdict at each size comes from paired repeats.** The candidate and the compiled reference run in alternating order, 30 times, and so does the baseline when one is given.
23|  - The candidate is `faster` when it wins at least 22 of the 30 pairs, a one-sided sign test at p < 0.01.
24|  - It is `slower` when it loses at least 22, and `same` otherwise.
25|
26|  This replaces the comparison of medians for the decode sizes too, since the same kernel timed twice differs by up to 5%.
27|- **The verdict per phase:**
28|  - a phase is `faster` when every one of its sizes is;
29|  - it is `slower` when any size is;
30|  - otherwise it is `not slower`.
31|
32|  `beats_compiled`, and `beats_baseline` against a baseline, are true when one phase is `faster` and neither is `slower`.
33|- **The hand-off** (`max_rows` in `spec.json`, `bench/grader/slots.py`). Inputs with more rows than `max_rows` run the slot's reference under `mx.compile`. G2 still checks every size.
34|  - On 2026-11-04 the compiled reference of each slot was bit-exact with the reference at all six sizes (`bench/micro/compiled_exact.py`, `results/runs/2026-11-04-handoff-check/`).
35|  - Above `max_rows` a hand-off runs the compiled reference itself, so it times `same` as the bar there, never better.
36|- **G3** (`bench/grader/time_candidates.py`, which writes `g3-vllm.json`):
37|  - **Workloads:** 1, 8 and 32 requests with 128-token prompts, and 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts.
38|  - **Measurements per run:** the decode step period, the prompt time and the whole-request time, over 5 shuffled repeats, up from 3.
39|  - **Faster and slower:** the two ranges over the repeats don't overlap.
40|  - **Why 5 repeats:** with 3 each, two identical engines' ranges miss each other by chance 1 time in 20 per direction. "Never slower" checks a phase 8 times (4 workloads, 2 bars), so a phase that changed nothing would fail about a third of the time. The first run under these rules showed it. A copy of experts attempt-7 with a hand-off at 59 rows came out `slower` on prompt time at 32 × 1,024, by 0.5% with ranges 16 ms apart, although above 59 rows it runs the compiled reference, whose own range overlapped the unchanged engine's (`results/runs/2026-11-04-handoff-check/`). With 5 repeats the chance is 1 in 252 per check, about 3% over 8.
41|  - **The pass rule:** against both the original model and the compiled reference, the decode step or the prompt time must be faster in every workload, neither may be slower in any, and no whole request may be slower.
42|- **The unchanged engine is vLLM's own.** The original model in G3 runs with Claude's step hooks, and with vLLM's engine inside the script's process. On 2026-11-04, alternating runs found it within −0.2% to +1.9% of vLLM with neither, inside the spread between repeats in every workload (`bench/micro/clean_vllm.py`, `results/runs/2026-11-04-clean-vllm/`).
43|
44|## Consequences
45|
46|- **Round 3 starts with no baseline.** Routing attempt-4 is `slower` at all three prefill sizes, 2.6 to 8.7 times the compiled reference's time. It fails G3 on prompt time at 8 and 32 requests. It becomes a starting point, so round 3's bar in every slot is the compiled reference.
47|- **A decode kernel no longer has to win at prefill sizes,** only to hand them off or not lose there. The attempt chooses the row count, so the boundary agent checks that the hand-off sits on the right side of 60 rows for the experts slot.
48|- **At prefill sizes, a slot with a hand-off is MLX's code, not the Muse agent's.** The claim for such an attempt is "faster decode, unchanged prefill".
49|- **Grader runs and G3 take longer.** Every attempt is now timed at three more sizes. G3 runs 5 repeats instead of 3, and its 32 × 1,024 workload adds at least 16 s per variant per repeat.
50|- **The decode verdict is stricter.** An attempt whose median beat the compiled reference by noise is now `same`.
51|- **Not covered:** prefill chunks of other sizes, and decode steps with other row counts. The boundary agent reports them; G3's four workloads are the end-to-end check.
52|- **At 1 request the whole-request time is noisy.** On 2026-11-04 its repeats spread 6% to 41%, so G3 there mostly says `same`, which passes the "never slower" test without showing a gain.
53|
54|## Considered options
55|
56|- **Faster in both phases.** The higher bar. A decode kernel would also have to beat MLX's large matrix kernels at 2,048 rows, which is not where the decode step loses its time. Not chosen.
57|- **Whole-request throughput alone.** Simple, but it lets a slower phase be traded for a faster one. surucuonur ruled that out.
58|- **Hand off to the uncompiled reference.** The prefill could then come out `slower` than the compiled reference wherever compiling helps; at 127 rows, routing's compiled reference takes 87 µs per layer against 102 µs uncompiled.
59|- **Keep the kernels in every call** (ADR 0010). The kernels could still branch on the row count inside themselves, but they couldn't use MLX's large-size kernels. surucuonur chose the hand-off.

1|# MobileMoE Bandwidth Study
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|How efficiently an inference engine turns an Apple Silicon GPU's memory bandwidth and compute into generated tokens when serving a small mixture-of-experts model.
6|
7|## Hardware limits
8|
9|**Peak bandwidth**:
10|The most bytes per second the GPU can read from unified memory, as rated by the manufacturer (about 200 GB/s on this project's M1 Pro).
11|_Avoid_: max bandwidth, memory speed
12|
13|**Peak compute**:
14|The most floating-point operations per second the GPU can perform (about 5.2 TFLOPS on the 16-core M1 Pro GPU).
15|_Avoid_: max compute, TFLOPS (as the name of the limit)
16|
17|**Achieved bandwidth**:
18|The bytes a decode step must read from memory (the weights it touches plus its share of cached attention state), divided by that step's duration.
19|_Avoid_: bandwidth usage, utilization (unqualified)
20|
21|**Arithmetic intensity**:
22|Floating-point operations performed per byte read from memory during a decode step.
23|_Avoid_: compute density, FLOPs/byte ratio
24|
25|**Ridge point**:
26|The arithmetic intensity at which peak bandwidth and peak compute meet (about 26 operations per byte here); below it a step is limited by bandwidth, above it by compute.
27|
28|**Roofline**:
29|The chart of achievable throughput against arithmetic intensity, capped by peak bandwidth on the left and peak compute on the right, with measured decode steps plotted beneath it.
30|
31|## Bottlenecks and fixes
32|
33|**Bandwidth-bound**:
34|A decode step whose achieved bandwidth is close to peak bandwidth.
35|
36|**Compute-bound**:
37|A decode step whose operation rate is close to peak compute.
38|
39|**Overhead-bound**:
40|A decode step far below both limits, because its time goes to work other than reading weights or doing arithmetic, such as launching GPU jobs, routing tokens to experts or scheduling.
41|_Avoid_: latency-bound, CPU-bound (unless the CPU specifically is the cause)
42|
43|**Bottleneck**:
44|The single cause, identified from measurements, that most limits throughput for a given workload.
45|_Avoid_: issue, slowness
46|
47|**Kernel**:
48|One program the GPU runs as a unit, such as one matrix product or one element-wise add; a decode step is a chain of hundreds of them, each with a fixed start-up cost.
49|_Avoid_: GPU job, op (for a kernel launch)
50|
51|**Occupancy**:
52|The share of the GPU's thread slots in use while it runs; low occupancy means most of the chip is idle even when the GPU counts as busy.
53|_Avoid_: GPU utilization (which only says the GPU had work)
54|
55|**Knock-out**:
56|A measurement in which one piece of the decode step is replaced by a stand-in that returns the right shape without GPU work; the time and bytes the step saves are that piece's cost.
57|_Avoid_: ablation
58|
59|**Baseline**:
60|The unmodified engine serving MobileMoE-S-QAT (int4), against which every fix is measured.
61|
62|**Fix**:
63|One change to the engine, the model code or the configuration, measured against the baseline under the same workload.
64|_Avoid_: optimization (for a change that hasn't been measured), tweak
65|
66|## Inference
67|
68|**Prefill**:
69|Processing a request's whole prompt through the model before its first token is generated, in chunks of up to the engine's token budget per pass (2,048 tokens here).
70|_Avoid_: prompt phase (say prefill, or prompt processing)
71|
72|**Decode step**:
73|One engine iteration that produces one new token for each request it includes.
74|
75|**Decode rows**:
76|The number of requests the engine actually advanced in one decode step; the batch size that matters for the roofline.
77|_Avoid_: batch size (unqualified), concurrency
78|
79|**Client concurrency**:
80|The number of requests the benchmark client keeps in flight; it caps decode rows but does not equal them.
81|_Avoid_: batch size
82|
83|## Mixture of experts
84|
85|**Expert**:
86|One of the interchangeable feed-forward blocks in a layer; MobileMoE-S has 60 routed experts per layer.
87|
88|**Active experts**:
89|The experts the router picks for one token in one layer (4 for MobileMoE-S).
90|_Avoid_: selected experts, top-k experts
91|
92|**Distinct experts**:
93|The number of different experts used by all decode rows together in one layer during one decode step; it decides how much expert weight data the step must read.
94|_Avoid_: unique experts, expert coverage
95|
96|## Models
97|
98|**MobileMoE-S**:
99|Meta's smallest on-device mixture-of-experts model (about 1.3B parameters in total, about 272M used per token), studied here in its SFT (full-precision) and QAT (int4) variants.
100|
101|**Muse Spark**:
102|Meta's hosted model, and the Muse agent in round 1.
103|
104|**Muse Wonder**:
105|Meta's most capable model family, in preview; its standard variant runs on Meta's Model API. The Muse agent in round 2.
106|
107|**Muse Wonder Full**:
108|The higher-capability variant of Muse Wonder, available only in Muse Code with a subscription; not used in this project.
109|
110|**Muse agent**:
111|The Meta model that chooses which pieces of the decode step to replace and writes their kernels, on the branch `muse-agent`: Muse Spark in round 1 and from round 3, Muse Wonder in round 2. It is never the model under study.
112|_Avoid_: Muse (alone), Meta agent
113|
114|**Muse Code**:
115|Meta's own coding agent for the terminal; the only program in which the Muse agent does its work in this project.
116|_Avoid_: Muse CLI, Meta Code
117|
118|**Muse agent session**:
119|A Muse Code session in which the Muse agent writes every turn, the lead's and every helper's, kept apart from Claude's work by its own branch, folder and commit trailer.
120|_Avoid_: Muse Spark session (round 2's model was Muse Wonder), guardrail (for the session itself), Meta mode
121|
122|## The Muse agent's work
123|
124|**Slot**:
125|One replaceable piece of the mixture-of-experts block (routing, combine, or the routed experts), with fixed inputs and outputs, that the Muse agent may replace with its own kernels.
126|_Avoid_: target (that is a slot the Muse agent has chosen), module
127|
128|**Round**:
129|One Muse agent session in which a swarm explores and then builds, writing in its own round folder, followed by Claude's independent measurement of what it produced. Once a round is finished, its files are frozen.
130|_Avoid_: iteration, cycle
131|
132|**Round folder**:
133|Where one round writes all its files: round 1 at the top of `muse-spark/`, each later round in `muse-spark/round-<N>/`.
134|
135|**Starting point**:
136|The plan each round from round 2 on begins with, drawn from the earlier rounds and Claude's measurement: each slot's baseline, or the attempt to start from where it has none, with its end-to-end effect; what is left to build; the refuted claims; and the territories to explore again.
137|_Avoid_: recap, retrospective
138|
139|**Improvement**:
140|An attempt that is faster than its bar in one phase, prefill or decode, and slower in neither; a faster decode step bought with a slower prefill is not one.
141|_Avoid_: speedup (for a change measured in one phase only)
142|
143|**Hand-off**:
144|An attempt's choice to run the compiled reference instead of its own kernels above a row count it names, so prefill-sized inputs stay on MLX's code.
145|_Avoid_: fallback
146|
147|**Baseline** (of a slot):
148|A slot's best attempt so far that passes the current G2 and that Claude's G3 accepted, named in Claude's measurement of the previous round; every new attempt for that slot must beat it in the same grader run. A slot may have none.
149|_Avoid_: reference (that is the original MLX code and its compiled version)
150|
151|**Swarm**:
152|All the agents of one round, the lead and its helpers, working toward one goal through shared documents that each of them reads and adds to.
153|_Avoid_: team, crew
154|
155|**Lead agent**:
156|The one agent of a swarm that starts the helpers, keeps the shared documents current, settles clashes and commits; it neither explores nor grades.
157|_Avoid_: orchestrator, main agent
158|
159|**Helper agent**:
160|An agent the lead starts: an explorer, the verifier, a builder or a boundary agent. It reports back and never commits.
161|_Avoid_: worker, subagent (when the role matters, not the mechanism)
162|
163|**Reminder agent**:
164|One of Muse Code's own background agents, which watch the lead's progress and may nudge it, for example to check a claim before it says it is done; the Muse agent's model writes their turns too, but they take no part in the work.
165|_Avoid_: helper (that is one the lead starts)
166|
167|**Exploration phase**:
168|The first part of a round, in which explorers map the code and the measurements and find where the decode step loses time.
169|
170|**Implementation phase**:
171|The second part of a round, in which builders write and grade solutions to the confirmed inefficiencies.
172|_Avoid_: hypothesis phase
173|
174|**Territory**:
175|The part of the code or the measurements that one explorer covers: a module, a single important file, or a measurement document.
176|_Avoid_: area, lens
177|
178|**Analysis**:
179|The swarm's shared account of the code, written during exploration: the context, how the territories feed each other, and the ranked inefficiencies, each with its cost and sources.
180|_Avoid_: diagnosis, findings (those are Claude's)
181|
182|**Inefficiency**:
183|One cause of lost time in the decode step: where it is in the code, what it costs, and what removing it should save. It is confirmed or refuted against its sources before anyone builds on it.
184|_Avoid_: issue, bottleneck (that is the single largest cause)
185|
186|**Hypothesis**:
187|A proposed solution to one inefficiency: the slot it replaces, the boundary it keeps and the saving it predicts, tested by competing attempts.
188|_Avoid_: strategy, plan
189|
190|**Boundary**:
191|What a solution must keep identical so that the steps before and after its slot work exactly as before: the slot's inputs and outputs, their dtypes, and the rounding points.
192|_Avoid_: interface (unqualified), contract
193|
194|**Attempt**:
195|One grader run of a solution a builder wrote, committed by the lead; attempts for a slot are numbered in order within each round and have no limit.
196|_Avoid_: try, submission, draft

3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur.*
4|
5|The hackathon rules require judges to tell what was built during the event, and by whom. This page lists every contributor to this repository, what each one made, and how to check it.
6|
7|## The contributors

9|| Who | What they made | Where it is | How it is marked |
10||---|---|---|---|
11|| **surucuonur** (the entrant) | Direction and every decision; ran the machine; started the Muse agent's sessions; reviewed the results | every commit | Author and committer of every commit |
12|| **Claude Code** (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) | The benchmark, grader and provenance code, the measurements, every write-up, and Muse Spark's brief and round skill | `bench/`, `claude/`, `tools/`, `.agents/skills/`, `README.md`, this page, and the Markdown in `results/` | Commits co-authored by `Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`, which GitHub shows as the `claude` account; a byline under each document's title |

14|| **Others, before the event** | vLLM, vllm-metal, mlx-lm, MLX, and Meta's MobileMoE-S weights | `third_party/` (pinned submodules) and the installed wheels; the weights are downloaded, not committed | Their own authors and licences |
15|
16|## How the work is kept apart
17|
18|Every commit is authored and committed by surucuonur. The `Co-Authored-By` trailer says whose work the content is:
19|
20|```
21|Claude's work                         The Muse agent's work
22|-------------                         ---------------------
23|branch: main                          branch: muse-agent
24|Author: surucuonur                    Author: surucuonur
25|Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5       Co-Authored-By: Muse Spark (Meta Model API)
26|  <noreply@anthropic.com>               <muse-spark@meta-model-api.invalid>      (round 1)
27|Claude-Session: <session link>        Co-Authored-By: Muse Wonder (Meta Model API)
28|never changes muse-spark/               <muse-wonder@meta-model-api.invalid>     (round 2 on)
29|                                      changes only muse-spark/
30|```
31|
32|The Muse agent works in Muse Code, Meta's own coding agent, which surucuonur starts with `tools/muse-agent/start.sh` ([ADR 0006](claude/adr/0006-muse-spark-in-muse-code.md)). That script is the only way to start one. It ran Muse Spark in round 1 and Muse Wonder in round 2 ([ADR 0008](claude/adr/0008-muse-wonder.md)), and runs Muse Spark's contributor model from round 3, with tool approvals off ([ADR 0012](claude/adr/0012-muse-spark-contributor-unattended.md)). Each round follows the skill [.agents/skills/muse-round/SKILL.md](.agents/skills/muse-round/SKILL.md), which Claude wrote and committed before the round that uses it. Its version number is in its header and its history in [its changelog](.agents/skills/muse-round/CHANGELOG.md), and each round records the version it ran. In it, the Muse agent works as a swarm ([ADR 0007](claude/adr/0007-muse-spark-swarm.md)):
33|- explorers map the code and the measurements into a shared analysis;
34|- builders write and grade competing kernels;
35|- the lead coordinates, and only the lead commits;
36|- both phases are tracked in shared documents in the round's folder.
37|
38|Rounds build on each other ([ADR 0009](claude/adr/0009-rounds-build-on-each-other.md)). Each round writes in its own folder, and once it is finished Claude tags its last commit `muse-round-<N>`, which freezes its files: round 1's tag is `muse-round-1`, on `60308aa`. From round 2 on, a round starts from the earlier rounds' results and Claude's G3, and each new attempt must beat its slot's best attempt so far in the same grader run.
39|
40|Six layers keep its work and Claude's from mixing:
41|
42|1. **Place.** The Muse agent has its own git worktree on `muse-agent` and writes only in `muse-spark/`, in the current round's folder. Its worktree has no `.env`. The launcher gives `muse` a home folder of its own, `~/.muse-spark`, so Muse Code finds none of surucuonur's personal skills and rules, Claude's included, and keeps its settings, account login and session logs there. In round 1 the API key went only to the `muse` process; from round 2 the session signs in to surucuonur's Muse Code subscription, and the launcher passes no key at all.
43|2. **Identity.** Every Muse agent commit carries its model's co-author, which the launcher gives the lead in its first prompt and the lead writes as the skill shows. The `.invalid` addresses are reserved and belong to no one (RFC 2606); Meta's models have no GitHub account, so we neither claim nor invent one.
44|3. **Hooks.** `tools/githooks/` refuses mixed commits: a Muse agent's co-author off `muse-agent`, Claude's on it, `muse-agent` commits without a Muse agent's co-author or outside `muse-spark/`, other commits inside it (merges of `muse-agent` excepted), and any staged API key. On `muse-agent` it also refuses any change to a finished round's files, and new files outside the current round's folder and `muse-spark/transcripts/`.
45|4. **Audit.** `tools/provenance_check.py` re-checks the whole history against the same rules, so a commit made around the hooks is caught.
46|5. **Evidence.** Muse Code logs every model call, tool run and edit of the lead, its helpers and Muse Code's own reminder agents. `tools/export_transcript.py` saves each session in `muse-spark/transcripts/`.
47|   - **What it keeps:** every agent's conversation, how each tool call was approved, and the model of every model call.
48|   - **What it drops:** Muse Code's own instructions.
49|   - It refuses a session that contains a key.
50|   - The audit checks that a Meta model made every call.
51|   - It writes into the worktree from any checkout, and skips sessions already exported.
52|6. **Independent grading.** The grader (`bench/grader/`) is Claude's; the Muse agent may run it but not change it, and it runs one GPU job at a time. Its results in the write-up come from re-running it, and G3, on the main checkout after the merge.
53|
54|**The removed API stage.** Before the agent session, Muse Spark was called through a Claude-written API pipeline: 2 calls, a strategy and one routing+combine kernel. That stage was removed so all of Muse Spark's results come from one method. Its commits remain in the history: `d14c4a3` (the brief), `48cb61f` and `8c0a9b0` (Muse Spark's answers), `6c0a0ba` and `2c71eb4` (their logs). The audit lists them under "before".
55|
56|**The deleted Claude Code stage.** From the tag `agent-era` until the move to Muse Code, Muse Spark worked as a Claude Code session powered by Meta's API ([ADR 0004](claude/adr/0004-muse-spark-as-claude-code-agent.md), [ADR 0005](claude/adr/0005-muse-spark-launcher-only-contributor-tier.md)). Its three sessions produced one strategy commit and one kernel attempt that was never graded. On 2026-11-02, surucuonur deleted that unpushed `muse-agent` branch and started over in Muse Code, so no graded result comes from that stage.
57|
58|## A Muse Spark model in Claude's session (2026-11-02)
59|
60|On 2026-11-02, before Meta's settings were confined to the launcher ([ADR 0005](claude/adr/0005-muse-spark-launcher-only-contributor-tier.md)), a switch that points Claude Code at Meta put Claude's own session in the main checkout on `muse-spark-1.3-contributor` for several turns.
61|- **What it saw:** those turns ran with Claude's configuration. They loaded Claude's memory notes and surucuonur's global instructions, and read this page, ADR 0004, the brief, the launcher and its settings. All of it went to Meta on the tier where Meta may train on it.
62|- **What it did:** its shell commands failed, and it wrote and committed nothing. No file in this repository comes from those turns.
63|- **What prevents it now:** Muse Spark runs only in Muse Code, started by `tools/muse-agent/start.sh`; no Claude Code configuration points at Meta.
64|
65|## Personal context in the first Muse Code smoke test (2026-11-03)
66|
67|Before round 1, Claude ran two short smoke tests with the launcher, at surucuonur's request. Each was a headless Muse Spark session in the worktree that only ran read-only checks: git status, the brief's first line, one MLX operation on the GPU and one read-only helper agent. A third test, after the move to a swarm (session `01a1a2eb-a2fd-79f1-a880-1d7b36e56322`), started two explorers. They wrote entries and log lines in a scratch folder outside `muse-spark/`, each added a note to the other's entry, and the folder was then deleted. None of the three committed anything. Between the second and third, surucuonur started one round session as a trial (`01a1a2b8-03a0-7890-baf7-9febe7b8d245`), on the round skill's version 1, and stopped it after 4 minutes; it wrote and committed nothing.
68|- **What went wrong in the first** (session `01a1a2a2-76ea-7fe3-95d8-7df76e209c74`):
69|  - The launcher then relied on Muse Code's settings for leaving personal skills and rules out, and they didn't work ([ADR 0006](claude/adr/0006-muse-spark-in-muse-code.md)).
70|  - The context of the lead and its helper held surucuonur's global instructions (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`) and the names and descriptions of 43 personal skills from `~/.agents/skills` and `~/.claude/skills`.
71|  - All of it went to Meta on the tier where Meta may train on it.
72|- **What it did:** the read-only checks; it wrote and committed nothing.
73|- **What prevents it now:** the launcher gives `muse` its own home folder. In the second smoke test (session `01a1a2a7-d562-76c3-a410-07629daf9bbc`), the lead and the helper saw only Muse Code's 25 bundled skills, its bundled plugin's skill and `muse-round`, and no rules file.

claude/findings/muse-round-1.md:5:In round 1 (2026-11-03), the Muse agent (Muse Spark, `muse-spark-1.3-contributor`) explored the decode step as a swarm, then wrote fused Metal kernels for three slots of the mixture-of-experts block. Its summary, [muse-spark/summary.md](../../muse-spark/summary.md), names one final attempt per slot. Each one passed the grader, and the summary predicted, from the per-slot timing, that together they would shorten the decode step by 0.54, 1.81 and 5.72 ms at 1, 8 and 32 requests.

claude/findings/muse-round-1.md:91:| round 1's prediction, all three | −0.54 | −1.81 | −5.72 |
claude/findings/muse-round-2.md:13:For experts it keeps MLX's reference. Its best experts kernel, attempt-7, was bit-exact and faster with 8 and 32 rows, but it was dropped for being slower with 1 row. The summary predicted the submission would shorten the decode step by 0.84 ms at 1, 8 and 32 requests.
claude/findings/muse-round-2.md:39:- **The submission (routing + combine), in vLLM:** −0.73 ms (−13%) with 1 request, −0.74 ms (−5%) with 8, **+0.53 ms (+2%) with 32**, against a prediction of −0.84 ms at each. combine's slowdown outweighs routing's saving with 32 requests.
claude/findings/muse-round-2.md:90:| round 2's prediction for the submission | −0.84 | −0.85 | −0.84 |
claude/findings/muse-round-2.md:154:- **What it missed:** its prediction for combine (−0.35 ms) and for the submission at 32 requests. The chained piece timing still doesn't show combine's cost in the step.

claude/findings/muse-round-2.md:20:G3 timed each kernel alone, the submission, experts attempt-7 added to it, round 1's three kernels and the compiled references, all in the same run. A last run timed every pairing of round 2's three kernels, to find where they interfere.
claude/findings/muse-round-2.md:37:- **routing attempt-4 passed G3 as it stood, on decode steps.** It is faster than both the unchanged model and the compiled reference at 1, 8 and 32 requests, in both engines. In vLLM it saves 0.47, 0.43 and 0.54 ms per step (8.7%, 3.0% and 1.8%). It is the project's first Muse kernel that passed every rule of its time. Over whole requests its gain is smaller, since it processes prompts 7–10% slower: throughput rises 10.2% with 1 request and 1.8% with 8, is flat with 32 and falls 3.5% with 32 requests of 1,024-token prompts ([section 5](#5-whole-requests-prompts-and-throughput)). Under the rule set after this measurement, that an improvement must hold in both phases ([ADR 0011](../adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)), it fails, so it is no baseline for round 3 ([For round 3](#for-round-3-baselines-and-starting-points)).
claude/findings/muse-round-2.md:38:- **combine attempt-1 fails G3.** The grader timed it faster than the compiled reference at every row count. In the model it is slower than the unchanged step with 32 requests (+1.05 ms in vLLM, +1.17 ms in plain MLX), and no faster than the compiled reference with 8.

claude/findings/muse-round-2.md:158:**The rule,** from round 3 ([ADR 0011](../adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)): a slot's baseline is its best attempt so far that passes the current G2, has `beats_compiled` true in the grader, and passes G3. Both of those now judge two phases, decode and prefill: faster in one, slower in neither, and in G3 no whole request slower, against the unchanged model and the compiled reference. An attempt that passes G2 but not the rest is a starting point, not a bar: making it the bar would ask a fix to beat it where it already wins.
claude/findings/muse-round-2.md:160:The current grader re-graded round 2's three kernels on 2026-11-04 (`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2/grade-phases-*.json`). Times are multiples of the compiled reference's, per layer:
claude/findings/muse-round-2.md:168:Round 3 has no baseline in any slot, so its bar is the compiled reference everywhere.
claude/findings/muse-round-2.md:171:1. **experts with 1 row.** attempt-7 keeps its 8- and 32-row speed and loses at 1 row, as every fused design in round 2 did (92 to 110 µs per layer chained, against 73 to 87 for the compiled reference, in round 2's runs). Round 2's summary suggests copying the reference's unfused structure exactly for small row counts.
claude/findings/muse-round-2.md:174:4. **Prefill speed.** From round 3 the grader times the prefill sizes and G3 times prompts and whole requests (ADR 0011). routing attempt-4 and experts attempt-7 are slower than the compiled reference at every prefill size; combine attempt-1 is faster. An attempt may keep inputs above a row count it names on the compiled reference (`max_rows`, in the brief). Claude checked that hand-off on a copy of experts attempt-7 with `max_rows` 59: bit-exact at all six sizes, and the `same` as the compiled reference at every prefill size (`results/runs/2026-11-04-handoff-check/`).

1. **Unmeasured costs free (prefill).** Caused in-round by the rules then in
  force: R1's grader tested decode sizes only (`muse-round-1.md:71`) under old
  G2 tolerances, and G3 timed decode steps only (`0010:44`, `muse-round-2.md:146`).

  prompts 6.6-14.5x slower cutting throughput 10-83%, routing prompts 7-10%
  slower costing 3.5% at 32x1024 (`muse-round-2.md:40`, `:134-:145`). Already
  constrained: 0010 fixed prefill *correctness* (bit-exact at 6 sizes,
  `0010:24-:31`); 0011 fixed prefill *speed* (6-size piece timing, `max_rows`
  hand-off, 4-workload G3 with prompt+whole-request, `0011:21-:41`) and the
  glossary now defines a one-phase gain as NOT an improvement (`GLOSSARY:139-141`).

  other decode row counts (`0011:51`), plus 6-41% noise in 1-request
  whole-request time (`0011:52`); and nothing in my territory gives the *round*
  an in-round end-to-end number before Claude's post-merge G3 (G3-after-merge
  is the standing split, `0006:49`, `PROVENANCE:52`).

  timing -0.54/-1.81/-5.72, measured +0.98/+0.16/-1.76 (`muse-round-1.md:5`,
  `:89`, `:91`); R2 predicted -0.84(-0.85)/-0.84, measured -0.726/-0.735/+0.527

  two measured non-additivities: R1 triple vs parts at 8 (+0.16 vs -1.93 parts)
  and 32 (-1.76 vs -5.03 parts, derived sums from `:83-:89`), "measured but not
